title: History and Perspectives of Psychology
objectives: Master History and Perspectives of Psychology for the Scientific Foundations of Psychology unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: analyzing conscious experience through introspection
how mental processes help organisms adapt to environment
behavioral, cognitive, biological, psychodynamic, sociocultural, humanistic

traps: Treating psychological perspectives as competing truths where one is right — AP tests that each perspective is a LENS emphasizing different factors; a psychologist choosing a perspective is choosing what to study, not claiming the others are wrong; explaining behavior fully often requires multiple perspectives; AP multiple choice frequently gives a scenario and asks WHICH perspective best explains it

title: Research Methods — Experiments, Correlations, Statistics
objectives: Master Research Methods — Experiments, Correlations, Statistics for the Scientific Foundations of Psychology unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: independent variable manipulated, dependent variable measured, confounds controlled
relationship between variables — does NOT prove causation
results unlikely due to chance; effect size: how large the difference actually is

traps: Confusing correlation with causation — AP tests this distinction relentlessly; a positive correlation between ice cream sales and drowning doesn't mean ice cream causes drowning (lurking variable: summer); experimental design controls for this by random assignment; AP free response frequently asks you to identify why a study cannot demonstrate causation and how you would redesign it as a true experiment

title: Biological Bases of Behavior — The Neuron
objectives: Master Biological Bases of Behavior — The Neuron for the Scientific Foundations of Psychology unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: all-or-none, travels down axon to synaptic terminal
chemical messengers crossing the synapse (acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin)
neurotransmitter reabsorbed by presynaptic neuron — SSRIs block this for serotonin

traps: Memorizing neurotransmitter lists without knowing their functions — AP tests SPECIFIC associations: dopamine → reward, Parkinson's, schizophrenia; serotonin → mood, anxiety, SSRIs; acetylcholine → memory, muscle movement, Alzheimer's; GABA → inhibition, anxiety; the free response frequently describes a symptom and asks which neurotransmitter system is involved; know the function AND the disorder associated with excess/deficit

title: The Brain — Structures and Functions
objectives: Master The Brain — Structures and Functions for the Biological Bases of Behavior unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: amygdala (emotion/fear), hippocampus (memory consolidation)
frontal (executive function, motor), parietal (somatosensory), temporal (auditory/language), occipital (visual)
reorganization after injury; critical periods for development

traps: Mixing up lobes and their functions — AP tests this with patient case studies; frontal lobe damage = impulse control and personality changes (Phineas Gage); temporal lobe damage = language comprehension issues (Wernicke's area); the AP question type is 'a patient shows symptom X — which brain area is most likely damaged?'; practice mapping symptoms to structures rather than memorizing the other direction

title: Genetics and Behavior — Nature vs. Nurture
objectives: Master Genetics and Behavior — Nature vs. Nurture for the Biological Bases of Behavior unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: proportion of variation in a trait explained by genetic differences — applies to POPULATIONS, not individuals
identical twins raised apart showing similar traits → genetic influence
environmental factors influencing gene expression without changing DNA sequence

traps: Treating heritability as saying genetics determines individual outcomes — heritability of 80% for height doesn't mean 80% of YOUR height is genetic; it means 80% of height VARIATION in the population is explained by genes; a poor diet can prevent you from reaching genetic potential; AP tests that heritability is a population statistic, not a statement about any individual's development

title: Sensation — Thresholds and Transduction
objectives: Master Sensation — Thresholds and Transduction for the Sensation and Perception unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: minimum stimulus detectable 50% of the time
minimum change detectable — Weber's Law: proportional to original stimulus
hits, misses, false alarms, correct rejections — sensitivity vs. response bias

traps: Confusing absolute threshold with difference threshold — ABSOLUTE: can you detect the stimulus at all? (light in a dark room); DIFFERENCE: can you detect that it CHANGED? (is this coffee sweeter?); Weber's Law applies only to the difference threshold; AP tests both with specific scenarios; signal detection theory is tested with the concept that sensitivity and criterion are SEPARATE — a surgeon and a nervous radiologist can have the same sensitivity but different false alarm rates

title: Perception — Top-Down Processing and Gestalt Principles
objectives: Master Perception — Top-Down Processing and Gestalt Principles for the Sensation and Perception unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: prior knowledge and expectations influencing perception (reading in context)
building perception from sensory data without prior knowledge
figure-ground, proximity, similarity, continuity, closure — organizing perception

traps: Treating perception as passive recording of reality — AP tests that perception is CONSTRUCTIVE; top-down processing means your brain fills in gaps, sometimes creating errors (moon illusion, perceptual set); the key AP insight is that two people with different schemas or expectations can perceive the same stimulus differently; free response questions about perception almost always require explaining how context or expectation influenced the result

title: Classical Conditioning — Pavlov and Applications
objectives: US → UR (unconditioned); CS + US → CS → CR (conditioned)
Extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination
Systematic desensitization using classical conditioning to treat phobias

sections.title: Classical Conditioning — Pavlov and Applications
traps: Identifying the CS when given a scenario — AP tests this with complex scenarios where you must identify which stimulus was originally neutral; the CS is the previously neutral stimulus that PREDICTS the US; in advertising, the product (originally neutral) is paired with attractive people (US for positive feelings) until the product alone (CS) causes desire (CR); always ask: what was neutral before conditioning began?

title: Operant Conditioning — Reinforcement and Punishment
objectives: Positive adds; negative removes; reinforcement increases behavior; punishment decreases behavior — 4 combinations

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: variable ratio produces highest response rate and greatest resistance to extinction
reinforcing successive approximations toward the target behavior

traps: Confusing negative reinforcement with punishment — NEGATIVE REINFORCEMENT increases behavior by removing something unpleasant (taking aspirin removes headache → you take aspirin more); PUNISHMENT decreases behavior; AP tests the 2x2 matrix: positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, positive punishment, negative punishment; categorizing a scenario into one of these four correctly is a standard multiple choice task

title: Memory — Encoding, Storage, and Retrieval
objectives: Master Memory — Encoding, Storage, and Retrieval for the Learning and Cognition unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: sensory → short-term/working → long-term memory
semantic (meaning) encoding most effective for long-term retention
context-dependent memory; mood-congruent memory; misinformation effect

traps: Treating forgetting as simple memory decay — AP tests MULTIPLE causes of forgetting: encoding failure (never stored properly), storage decay (trace fades), retrieval failure (can't access), interference (proactive: old info blocks new; retroactive: new info blocks old), and motivated forgetting; the misinformation effect (Loftus) is specifically tested — memory is RECONSTRUCTIVE, not like a video recording; eyewitness testimony is unreliable for this reason

title: Piaget's Cognitive Development Stages
objectives: Schema, assimilation, accommodation — how children update understanding

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: object permanence; Preoperational (2-7): egocentric, no conservation
conservation, reversibility; Formal operational (12+): abstract reasoning

traps: Memorizing stages without understanding the TEST scenarios — AP gives a SPECIFIC child behavior and asks which stage; preoperational children fail conservation tasks (think a tall narrow glass has more water than a short wide one) BECAUSE they focus on one dimension (centration) and can't reverse the action mentally; knowing the stage name is not enough — you must know the specific cognitive limitation being tested

title: Social Development — Attachment and Identity
objectives: Master Social Development — Attachment and Identity for the Developmental Psychology unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: contact comfort more important than feeding for attachment
secure vs. insecure (anxious, avoidant) attachment styles
each with a psychosocial crisis (trust vs. mistrust, identity vs. role confusion)

traps: Confusing Erikson with Piaget or Kohlberg — Erikson is PSYCHOSOCIAL (emotional/social challenges across lifespan); Piaget is COGNITIVE (reasoning ability in childhood); Kohlberg is MORAL reasoning; AP presents a scenario and asks which theorist's framework best explains it; identify the domain: is it about thinking ability (Piaget), social/emotional challenge (Erikson), or moral judgment (Kohlberg)?

title: Motivation — Theories and Hunger
objectives: Master Motivation — Theories and Hunger for the Motivation, Emotion, and Personality unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: physiological → safety → love → esteem → self-actualization
biological needs creating drives that motivate behavior to restore homeostasis
overjustification effect — rewarding intrinsically motivated behavior can reduce it

traps: Treating Maslow as a strict sequence everyone follows — AP tests the OVERJUSTIFICATION EFFECT as the most commonly tested motivation concept; if you reward a child who already loves reading (intrinsic motivation) with money, they may lose the intrinsic motivation; removing the reward leaves them less motivated than before; this counterintuitive result is AP's favorite motivation question

title: Emotion — Theories and Expression
objectives: Master Emotion — Theories and Expression for the Motivation, Emotion, and Personality unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: physiological response first → then emotion (we are afraid because we run)
physiological and emotional response simultaneously, independently
arousal + cognitive label = emotion — same arousal can produce different emotions

traps: Confusing James-Lange with common sense — common sense says we see a bear, feel fear, then run; James-Lange reverses it: we see a bear, run, THEN feel fear (because we notice we're running); AP tests this by presenting a scenario and asking which theory it best illustrates; two-factor theory is tested with the Schachter-Singer adrenaline experiment — misattributing arousal to a situation produces stronger emotion

title: Psychological Disorders — Classification and Diagnosis
objectives: Master Psychological Disorders — Classification and Diagnosis for the Clinical Psychology — Disorders and Treatment unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: diagnostic criteria requiring impairment in functioning
GAD, phobias, panic disorder, OCD, PTSD — distinct presentations
major depressive disorder vs. bipolar I and II — episode type differences

traps: Confusing OCD with OCPD or confusing phobia with PTSD — AP tests SPECIFIC diagnostic criteria; OCD requires obsessions AND compulsions with insight that they're irrational; PTSD requires a traumatic event and includes flashbacks/avoidance; phobias are disproportionate fear of specific objects; major depression requires 5 of 9 symptoms for 2 weeks; free response often describes symptoms and asks you to identify the specific disorder with justification

title: Biomedical Treatments
objectives: Master Biomedical Treatments for the Clinical Psychology — Disorders and Treatment unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: SSRIs block serotonin reuptake; SNRIs add norepinephrine
block dopamine receptors — explaining both therapeutic effect and side effects
effective for severe depression when medication fails; how it works is unclear

traps: Explaining drug effects without connecting to neurotransmitters — AP free response requires the MECHANISM: SSRIs increase serotonin in the synapse by blocking reuptake (not by producing more serotonin); antipsychotics work by BLOCKING dopamine receptors (the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia); always trace: drug action → neurotransmitter effect → symptom change; stopping at 'it increases serotonin' without explaining how earns partial credit

title: Psychological Therapies — CBT and Beyond
objectives: Master Psychological Therapies — CBT and Beyond for the Clinical Psychology — Disorders and Treatment unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: identifying and challenging irrational thoughts; behavioral component changing reinforcement patterns
bringing unconscious conflicts to consciousness through free association and dream analysis
unconditional positive regard, empathy, genuineness — facilitating self-actualization

traps: Treating therapy types as interchangeable — AP tests MATCHING therapy to disorder: CBT is evidence-based for anxiety, depression, OCD; systematic desensitization (classical conditioning) for phobias; token economies (operant conditioning) for institutional settings; psychoanalysis for insight into unconscious patterns; free response gives a client description and asks which therapy would be most appropriate AND why based on theoretical principles

title: Social Influence — Conformity and Obedience
objectives: Master Social Influence — Conformity and Obedience for the Social Psychology unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: people conform to obviously wrong group answers — normative social influence
65% administered maximum shocks — situational power over moral behavior
overestimating disposition, underestimating situation in explaining others' behavior

traps: Treating Milgram as about individual cruelty — AP tests the SITUATIONAL explanation: most people administered shocks not because they were sadistic but because of situational pressures (authority, incremental escalation, responsibility diffusion); the lesson is that ordinary people can do terrible things in the right situational context — this is the fundamental attribution error reversed; AP rewards recognizing the power of situations over dispositions

title: Song Dynasty China — Bureaucracy and Innovation
objectives: Civil service exam expanding bureaucracy beyond aristocracy
Neo-Confucianism blending Confucian ethics with Buddhist/Daoist metaphysics

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: fast-ripening rice enabling population growth

traps: Treating the Song as militarily strong — the Song were economically and culturally dominant but MILITARILY weak, paying tribute to northern nomads; AP tests the contrast between economic prosperity and military vulnerability

title: Dar al-Islam — Political Fragmentation, Cultural Unity
objectives: Shared Islamic law, Arabic scholarship, and pilgrimage creating cultural cohesion despite political division

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: fragmentation into regional sultanates
Baghdad as intellectual center translating Greek texts

traps: Assuming political fragmentation weakened Islamic culture — AP tests that cultural and commercial unity persisted DESPITE political splintering; the umma (community of believers) transcended political borders

title: South and Southeast Asia — Hinduism, Buddhism, and Trade
objectives: Vijayanagara (Hindu) and Delhi Sultanate (Muslim) coexisting in South Asia
Srivijaya and Majapahit using Indian Ocean trade to fund maritime empires

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: local traditions blending with imported Hinduism/Buddhism/Islam

traps: Expecting religious uniformity in Southeast Asia — AP tests syncretism: rulers adopted Indian religious legitimacy while populations maintained local practices; Islam in Southeast Asia was famously flexible compared to the Middle East

title: Mali Empire — Trans-Saharan Trade and Islam
objectives: Griots preserving oral history as alternative to written record

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Mali controlling gold fields, Saharan routes carrying salt south
pilgrimage to Mecca demonstrating wealth and spreading Islamic prestige

traps: Thinking Mali's power was primarily military — it was COMMERCIAL; control of trade routes, not conquest armies, explains Mali's dominance; AP tests that trans-Saharan trade, not military expansion, was the engine of West African state power

title: The Americas Before European Contact — Aztec and Inca
objectives: Both empires without writing systems or iron — AP tests alternative state-building methods

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: chinampas agriculture, tribute empire, human sacrifice as political tool
mit'a labor system, quipu record-keeping, road network integrating conquered peoples

traps: Assuming Aztec and Inca were similar — they used opposite integration strategies: Aztec ruled through tribute and fear, allowing local autonomy; Inca physically relocated populations (mitmaq) for integration; AP tests these distinct models

title: Comparing Postclassical States — Patterns of Continuity
objectives: Master Comparing Postclassical States — Patterns of Continuity for the The Global Tapestry (c. 1200–c. 1450) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Confucian bureaucracy, Islamic law, Hindu caste — all persisting across political change
new religions spreading along trade routes alter cultural landscapes
distinguishing change from continuity within a time period

traps: Treating all continuities as evidence of stagnation — AP tests that continuities (like Confucian civil service) are CHOICES that explain stability; arguing something is 'unchanged' requires explaining WHY elites maintained it, not just noting it persisted

title: The Silk Roads — Goods, Ideas, and Disease
objectives: Luxury goods (silk, spices, porcelain) moving east-west; silver and horses moving east
Buddhism, Islam, and Christianity spreading along trade corridors

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: bubonic plague traveling Silk Roads from Central Asia to Europe/Middle East

traps: Listing only goods when asked about Silk Road effects — AP consistently tests the spread of DISEASE and RELIGION as equally important consequences; a complete answer addresses cultural and biological exchange, not just commerce

title: The Mongol Empire — Destruction, Unification, and the Pax Mongolica
objectives: Master The Mongol Empire — Destruction, Unification, and the Pax Mongolica for the Networks of Exchange (c. 1200–c. 1450) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: destruction of Baghdad (1258) ending Abbasid Caliphate
relative peace across Eurasia enabling long-distance trade
Ilkhanate converting to Islam, Yuan adopting Chinese administration

traps: Treating Mongols as only destroyers — AP tests the DUAL nature: initial destruction followed by facilitation of trade; the Pax Mongolica allowed Marco Polo's travels and Ibn Battuta's journeys; destruction and trade facilitation are both correct and must be balanced

title: Indian Ocean Trade — Monsoon Routes and Swahili Coast
objectives: Master Indian Ocean Trade — Monsoon Routes and Swahili Coast for the Networks of Exchange (c. 1200–c. 1450) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: seasonal reversal enabling predictable sailing schedules
African merchants integrated into Indian Ocean network
Tamil, Arab, Chinese traders maintaining enclaves in foreign ports

traps: Overlooking African agency in Indian Ocean trade — Swahili merchants were active participants, not passive recipients; AP tests that Kilwa's wealth came from controlling gold trade from Zimbabwe; African merchants had commercial sophistication equal to Arab and Indian counterparts

title: Trans-Saharan Trade — Gold, Salt, and Slaves
objectives: Camel domestication enabling Saharan crossing (the 'ship of the desert')
West African gold funding Islamic scholarship and architecture in Mali/Songhai
Enslaved people as trade commodity alongside gold and salt — trans-Saharan slavery predating Atlantic

sections.title: Trans-Saharan Trade — Gold, Salt, and Slaves
traps: Ignoring slavery in trans-Saharan trade — AP tests that enslaved Africans were a significant trade commodity BEFORE the Atlantic slave trade; denying this continuity earns partial credit at best; the trans-Saharan slave trade differed from Atlantic (less racially defined, more integrated)

title: The Role of Technology in Expanding Trade Networks
objectives: Magnetic compass and astrolabe improving maritime navigation
Lateen sail enabling sailing against the wind
Paper money (China) and bills of exchange reducing risks of long-distance commerce

sections.title: The Role of Technology in Expanding Trade Networks
traps: Attributing trade expansion solely to political stability — AP tests that TECHNOLOGY (compass, lateen sail) enabled sailors to take routes previously impossible; credit for Mongol peace alone misses the maritime revolution happening simultaneously in the Indian Ocean

title: Cultural Consequences of Exchange — Diffusion and Resistance
objectives: Buddhism declining in India while spreading through Silk Roads to East/Southeast Asia
Islam spreading through merchant networks, not conquest, in sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Chinese suspicion of foreign merchants, European fear of Islamic learning

traps: Assuming cultural diffusion was always welcomed — AP tests RESISTANCE as equally important: Chinese xenophobia, Japanese selective borrowing, Catholic Church condemning Islamic philosophy; a strong LEQ acknowledges that exchange was contested and selective, not automatic

title: Ottoman Empire — Gunpowder, Devshirme, and Expansion
objectives: Master Ottoman Empire — Gunpowder, Devshirme, and Expansion for the Land-Based Empires (c. 1450–c. 1750) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: gunpowder artillery defeating Byzantine walls
enslaved Christian boys trained as janissaries and administrators
non-Muslim communities governing themselves under Ottoman sovereignty

traps: Treating the Ottomans as purely military — AP tests the ADMINISTRATIVE innovations: devshirme created loyalty to the sultan over ethnic/family ties; millet system enabled control of diverse populations without forced conversion; military success depended on these administrative solutions

title: Safavid Empire — Shi'a Islam as State Identity
objectives: Forced conversion to Twelver Shi'a Islam distinguishing Safavids from Sunni neighbors
Isfahan as architectural showpiece demonstrating imperial legitimacy

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Battle of Chaldiran (1514) — Sunni-Shi'a split becoming geopolitical

traps: Treating Ottoman-Safavid conflict as purely political — AP tests that the Sunni-Shi'a divide was INSTRUMENTALIZED: Safavids converted Persia to Shi'a to create a distinct identity separate from Ottoman religious authority; the split had theological origins but geopolitical consequences

title: Mughal Empire — Akbar's Tolerance and Revenue Systems
objectives: Taj Mahal as symbol of Mughal cultural synthesis — Persian, Indian, Islamic architecture

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: syncretic religious policy removing jizya tax on non-Muslims
local revenue collectors keeping a share, funding central state

traps: Presenting Akbar as simply 'tolerant' — AP tests that tolerance was a POLITICAL STRATEGY for ruling a majority-Hindu empire; removing jizya reduced resentment and expanded the tax base; later rulers (Aurangzeb) reversed this and destabilized the empire, proving Akbar's policy was functionally necessary

title: Qing Dynasty — Manchu Rule and Han Chinese Continuity
objectives: Master Qing Dynasty — Manchu Rule and Han Chinese Continuity for the Land-Based Empires (c. 1450–c. 1750) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.term: Manchu minority ruling Han Chinese majority
terms.def: adopting Confucian bureaucracy for legitimacy
Han men required to wear Manchu hairstyle as submission symbol
neighboring states sending gifts to Beijing acknowledging Chinese supremacy

traps: Confusing Qing with Ming — the Qing were MANCHU conquerors who MAINTAINED the civil service exam to co-opt Han elites; AP tests this tension: Manchu rulers kept enough Confucian structure to rule effectively while imposing enough Manchu customs to assert dominance

title: Russian Empire — Expansion East and Westernization
objectives: Ivan the Terrible centralizing power, defeating Mongol successor states
Cossacks enabling eastward expansion into Siberia for fur trade

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: St. Petersburg, European dress, bureaucratic reform

traps: Treating Russian expansion as uniquely aggressive — AP tests the COMPARISON: Russia's land-based expansion east mirrors Spanish maritime expansion west; both used military technology to conquer indigenous peoples; both integrated conquered peoples into revenue-extracting systems

title: Gunpowder Empires — Common Patterns and Differences
objectives: Gunpowder artillery enabling centralized states to defeat decentralized feudal/nomadic opponents
All major land empires used some form of military slavery or professional army loyal to ruler

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: overextension, succession crises, rising provincial autonomy

traps: Treating all gunpowder empires as identical — AP tests specific differences: Ottomans used devshirme; Mughals used Rajput alliance; Qing used examination system to co-opt Chinese elites; the MECHANISMS of legitimacy differed even when the gunpowder technology was shared

title: European Maritime Expansion — Causes and Technology
objectives: Caravel ship + magnetic compass + astrolabe enabling open-ocean sailing

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Portuguese systematic exploration of African coast
spice trade profits, Christian missionary impulse, competition between states

traps: Listing only economic motives for exploration — AP tests the INTERACTION of motives: religion, glory, and profit were inseparable in European thinking; a complete explanation notes that Portuguese exploration was state-sponsored (unlike private merchants) because the profits were too large and risks too high for individuals

title: The Columbian Exchange — Biological Consequences
objectives: Horses transforming Plains Indian cultures — an unintended consequence of Spanish conquest

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: smallpox, measles causing 50-90% indigenous population collapse
maize, potato, tomato enabling European population growth

traps: Presenting the Columbian Exchange as balanced or positive — AP tests the ASYMMETRY: indigenous peoples had no immunity to Eurasian diseases; crop transfers helped Europe more than the Americas in population terms; the exchange enabled European colonization by eliminating the labor that would have resisted it

title: Spanish Colonialism — Encomienda and Casta System
objectives: Master Spanish Colonialism — Encomienda and Casta System for the Transoceanic Interconnections (c. 1450–c. 1750) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Spanish granted indigenous labor in exchange for Christian conversion obligation
forced labor in silver mines (Potosí) — millions of indigenous workers drafted
racial hierarchy with peninsulares at top, enslaved Africans at bottom

traps: Treating encomienda as simply slavery — encomienda was technically a LABOR TRIBUTE system, not ownership; AP tests the distinction: encomenderos couldn't sell the people, only extract labor; in practice it functioned like slavery, but the legal structure mattered for how the Church interacted with the system

title: Atlantic Slave Trade — Scale, Causes, and Effects
objectives: Master Atlantic Slave Trade — Scale, Causes, and Effects for the Transoceanic Interconnections (c. 1450–c. 1750) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: European goods to Africa, enslaved Africans to Americas, raw materials to Europe
12-15% mortality rate; approximately 12.5 million enslaved Africans transported
some elites enriched by selling captives to Europeans

traps: Attributing the slave trade solely to European demand — AP tests African AGENCY: some West African elites actively participated as sellers; this doesn't reduce European culpability but shows the trade was enabled by African political fragmentation and elite profit-seeking; avoiding this complexity earns partial credit

title: Silver Trade — Global Economy Begins
objectives: Master Silver Trade — Global Economy Begins for the Transoceanic Interconnections (c. 1450–c. 1750) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: 80% of world silver supply coming from Spanish colonial mines

terms.term: Silver flowing to China via Manila Galleons
terms.def: Chinese tax system requiring silver payment creating global demand
too much silver chasing same goods

traps: Treating silver trade as just a Spanish story — AP tests that the DESTINATION of silver explains global connections: Chinese demand pulled silver east; Spanish silver funded European wars; inflation destabilized Spanish economy; the silver trade is the first genuinely global economic system and AP tests its multiple effects simultaneously

title: Coercive Labor Systems Compared
objectives: Master Coercive Labor Systems Compared for the Transoceanic Interconnections (c. 1450–c. 1750) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: encomienda tied to land and Christian obligation; chattel slavery was permanent racial hereditary status
temporary bondage used in British colonies after slavery ended
coerced labor enabling plantation agriculture across different colonial systems

traps: Using 'slavery' as a catch-all term — AP awards higher scores for distinguishing labor systems: encomienda, mita, chattel slavery, and indenture had different legal statuses, racial implications, and demographic consequences; a DBQ comparing labor systems requires these distinctions to score a 7

title: Resistance to Colonial Rule
objectives: Master Resistance to Colonial Rule for the Transoceanic Interconnections (c. 1450–c. 1750) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: escaped enslaved Africans establishing autonomous settlements (Jamaica, Suriname)
Pueblo peoples expelling Spanish from New Mexico for 12 years
incorporating African/indigenous practices into Catholic forms

traps: Treating colonized peoples as passive victims — AP tests AGENCY in resistance: Maroon communities successfully negotiated treaties with colonial governments; Pueblo Revolt is the most successful indigenous uprising against European colonizers; resistance took both violent and cultural forms, and AP expects both in an analysis

title: The Fur Trade and Northern Colonialism
objectives: Beaver pelt demand driving French-indigenous trade networks into the interior

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: alliance-based colonialism dependent on indigenous knowledge and labor
French integrated with indigenous peoples rather than replacing them

traps: Treating all European colonialism as identical — AP tests DIFFERENCES in colonial models: French depended on indigenous intermediaries and intermarried (métis); Spanish imposed replacement colonialism; British plantation model imported African labor; these distinctions explain different demographic outcomes and resistance patterns

title: The Enlightenment and Atlantic Revolutions
objectives: How Enlightenment ideas traveled through print culture to Atlantic world

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: natural rights, social contract, right to revolution
separation of powers as guard against tyranny

traps: Treating the Enlightenment as the single cause of Atlantic revolutions — AP tests MATERIAL causes alongside ideological: American Revolution driven by taxation without representation (economic) + Enlightenment ideas; Haitian Revolution driven by slavery's brutality (material) + French revolutionary ideals; ideas alone rarely cause revolutions

title: American and French Revolutions — Outcomes Compared
objectives: Both inspired by Enlightenment but produced opposite outcomes — why?

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: conservative revolution preserving property rights, creating republican government
radical revolution destroying aristocracy, ending in Napoleon's authoritarianism

traps: Treating these revolutions as equally radical — AP tests that the American Revolution was CONSERVATIVE (preserving British legal traditions, protecting property including enslaved people); the French was radical (abolishing aristocracy, universal male citizenship); this distinction explains why America stabilized quickly and France cycled through regimes

title: Haitian Revolution — The Exception That Tests the Rule
objectives: Only successful slave revolution in history — Toussaint L'Ouverture's leadership
French abolition of slavery (1794) creating the condition for Black soldiers fighting FOR France
Haiti inspiring fear in slaveholder societies worldwide, restricting its diplomatic recognition

sections.title: Haitian Revolution — The Exception That Tests the Rule
traps: Presenting Haiti as simply 'inspired by the French Revolution' — AP tests the IRONY: France's Revolution proclaimed universal rights but maintained slavery; Haiti forced the question of whether those rights applied to enslaved Africans; Napoleon's decision to reinstate slavery triggered the final uprising; causation runs from French contradiction, not French inspiration

title: Latin American Independence — Creole Revolutions
objectives: Creoles (American-born Spaniards) leading revolutions, not indigenous or mestizo populations
Napoleon's invasion of Spain (1808) removing the legitimating authority colonial loyalty depended on

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.term: Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín
terms.def: military campaigns connecting South America

traps: Assuming Latin American revolutions were socially radical like Haiti — AP tests that they were CREOLE revolutions preserving the racial hierarchy; indigenous and African populations rarely benefited; independence transferred power from peninsulares to creoles, not to the majority populations; this explains persistent inequality after independence

title: Industrial Revolution — Britain First, Why?
objectives: Enclosure movement creating mobile landless labor force available for factory work
Patent system protecting inventors; capital markets funding investment

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Britain's natural resources concentrated near navigable water

traps: Listing only coal and geography as causes — AP tests SOCIAL CONDITIONS: the enclosure movement is the hidden cause that created a dispossessed labor force willing to work in factories; without landless workers desperate for wages, machinery without operators changes nothing; demographic and property law changes enabled industrialization as much as resources

title: Social Effects of Industrialization
objectives: Master Social Effects of Industrialization for the Revolutions (c. 1750–c. 1900) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Manchester growing from 25,000 to 300,000 in 50 years
factory discipline, child labor, 14-hour days
factory owners, managers, professionals creating new social layer

traps: Focusing only on negative effects — AP tests that industrialization created the MIDDLE CLASS as a genuinely new social group with new values (thrift, hard work, separate spheres for women); responses to industrialization (socialism, labor unions, reform movements) are as important as the conditions they responded to

title: Nationalism — Unification and Fragmentation
objectives: Master Nationalism — Unification and Fragmentation for the Revolutions (c. 1750–c. 1900) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Bismarck using 'blood and iron' — wars against Denmark, Austria, France
Cavour's diplomacy + Garibaldi's military campaign
Greek independence, Balkan crises

traps: Treating nationalism as always a unifying force — AP tests that nationalism was SIMULTANEOUSLY fragmenting (breaking apart Ottoman and Habsburg empires) and consolidating (unifying Germany and Italy); which function it performed depended on whether the group was a majority or minority within an existing political unit

title: Abolitionism and the End of the Slave Trade
objectives: Haitian Revolution making slaveholders fear abolition; American South defending slavery as 'positive good'
British navy patrolling Atlantic after 1807 — enforcement gap between law and practice

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: evangelical Christianity + Enlightenment rights rhetoric + economic argument (free labor more productive)

traps: Crediting abolitionism solely to moral progress — AP tests ECONOMIC arguments: British industrialists argued free laborers consumed more goods (creating markets); Caribbean planters were losing competitiveness; moral arguments were effective because they aligned with economic interests of industrial capitalism; purely moral explanations are incomplete for AP

title: New Imperialism — Causes and the Scramble for Africa
objectives: Master New Imperialism — Causes and the Scramble for Africa for the Consequences of Industrialization (c. 1750–c. 1900) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: need for raw materials, markets for manufactured goods, investment outlets
nationalism and prestige driving competition between European powers
quinine (malaria prevention), steam power, repeating rifles enabling interior conquest

traps: Using 'economic greed' as the sole cause — AP tests the interaction of causes: a country could profit from trade without colonization; the political competition between European powers (fear of being left behind) drove the PACE and COMPREHENSIVENESS of colonization beyond what pure economics required; technology enabled what competition demanded

title: Imperialism in Asia — India and China Compared
objectives: Master Imperialism in Asia — India and China Compared for the Consequences of Industrialization (c. 1750–c. 1900) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: direct colonial rule after 1857 Sepoy Mutiny; railways, English education, legal system
'semicolonial' — unequal treaties, extraterritoriality, treaty ports without formal annexation
resisting colonization through Meiji industrialization — the exception proving the rule

traps: Treating China and India as experiencing identical imperialism — AP tests the distinction: India was COLONIZED (direct rule, British governor-general); China was SEMI-COLONIZED (kept nominal sovereignty but lost economic and legal autonomy); this distinction matters for explaining nationalist responses — Indian Congress vs. Chinese Qing weakness

title: Responses to Imperialism — Accommodation and Resistance
objectives: Master Responses to Imperialism — Accommodation and Resistance for the Consequences of Industrialization (c. 1750–c. 1900) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: selective Westernization as strategy to avoid colonization
educated elite using British legal framework to demand rights
xenophobic popular resistance to foreign presence in China

traps: Categorizing responses as simply 'resistant' or 'collaborative' — AP tests the SPECTRUM: Meiji Japan selectively adopted Western institutions (technology, military) while rejecting Western political control; Indian educated elites used British education against British rule; these sophisticated responses require analyzing what was adopted and what was rejected, and why

title: Economic Imperialism — Export Economies and Dependency
objectives: Master Economic Imperialism — Export Economies and Dependency for the Consequences of Industrialization (c. 1750–c. 1900) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: colonies forced into single cash crops (cotton in Egypt, rubber in Congo)
railroads running from interior to coast, not between cities
Indian textile industry destroyed by cheap British manufactured cloth

traps: Treating colonial economic development as beneficial modernization — AP tests DE-INDUSTRIALIZATION: India had sophisticated textile manufacturing before British rule; British tariffs protecting Lancashire mills while flooding Indian markets destroyed it; the infrastructure argument (railroads benefited India) ignores that it was designed for extraction, not internal development

title: Migration in the Industrial Age
objectives: Indian and Chinese contract labor (indenture) replacing enslaved labor in Caribbean and Pacific

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: 50+ million to Americas (1850-1914) fleeing poverty and persecution
rural to urban across industrializing regions

traps: Treating all migration as voluntary — AP tests coercion spectrum: chattel slavery → indenture → contract labor → 'voluntary' migration driven by economic desperation; indentured workers technically consented but were often deceived about conditions; AP asks you to analyze the DEGREE of coercion across different labor migration systems

title: Social Darwinism and Racism as Imperial Ideology
objectives: Herbert Spencer applying evolutionary theory to justify racial hierarchy ('survival of the fittest' society)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Kipling's poem presenting imperialism as civilizing mission
skull measurements, IQ testing used to legitimize subjugation

traps: Treating racist ideology as simply hypocritical cover for economic interests — AP tests that elites GENUINELY believed Social Darwinist claims; ideology shaped policy (separate education, restrictions on intermarriage); the economic and ideological motivations reinforced each other rather than one being real and the other fake

title: Women's Rights Movements in the 19th Century
objectives: Industrialization creating middle-class women with time and literacy for activism

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Declaration of Sentiments using Declaration of Independence language — deliberate rhetorical strategy
suffrage movement (political rights) vs. socialist feminism (economic equality)

traps: Treating women's rights as a purely Western phenomenon — AP tests that women organized across colonized world simultaneously; Indian women's organizations, Egyptian feminist union emerged in this period; the suffrage question was complicated by colonial women demanding rights that colonial men denied them, creating tensions within nationalist movements

title: Causes of World War I — MAIN and the Alliance System
objectives: Alliance system converting local conflict into continental war (Austria-Serbia → world war)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Serbian nationalism threatening Austro-Hungarian multi-ethnic empire
competition over colonies creating tensions between European powers

traps: Memorizing MAIN as four equal causes — AP tests the INTERACTION: militarism made war seem winnable; alliances made it spread; imperialism created the rivalries; nationalism provided the trigger (assassination); the alliance system is the MECHANISM that turned a regional crisis into world war; treating them as separate misses the causal chain

title: World War I — Total War and Its Effects
objectives: Master World War I — Total War and Its Effects for the Global Conflict (c. 1900–present) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: military stalemate created by industrial weapons outpacing military tactics
women in factories, rationing, propaganda
Ottoman deportation and massacre of Armenian Christians (1915-1923)

traps: Focusing only on the Western Front — AP tests GLOBAL dimensions: colonial soldiers from India, Africa, Southeast Asia fought for European powers; the war in the Middle East created the modern map through Sykes-Picot Agreement; the Armenian Genocide established the template for 20th century genocides; WWI was genuinely world-spanning

title: The Russian Revolution — Two Revolutions, One Year
objectives: Master The Russian Revolution — Two Revolutions, One Year for the Global Conflict (c. 1900–present) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: tsarist regime collapsed under war pressure and food shortages
Bolsheviks seizing power promising 'Peace, Land, Bread'
vanguard party, immediate revolution in agrarian society

traps: Treating the Russian Revolution as inevitable — AP tests CONTINGENCY: the February Revolution was spontaneous and Tsar Nicholas could have survived with minimal reform; the Bolsheviks succeeded because they made specific promises (land to peasants, end to war) that the Provisional Government refused to make; outcomes depended on decisions, not historical laws

title: Rise of Fascism — Italy and Germany
objectives: Hitler's legal rise to power through elections, then consolidation through emergency laws

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: hyperinflation (Germany), unemployment, perceived national humiliation enabling extremist appeal
ultranationalism, racial hierarchy, anti-Marxist

traps: Treating fascism as pure economic desperation — AP tests that the MIDDLE CLASS was fascism's core support, not the unemployed poor (who voted communist); fear of communist revolution drove middle-class professionals to fascist parties; economic crisis explains the opening but class anxiety explains which option people chose

title: World War II — Global Scope and the Holocaust
objectives: Master World War II — Global Scope and the Holocaust for the Global Conflict (c. 1900–present) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Japan's imperial expansion in Asia preceding European war by years
systematic genocide of 6 million Jews plus Roma, disabled, political opponents
ideologically incompatible powers (US democracy, Soviet communism) unified by common enemy

traps: Treating the Holocaust as separate from the war — AP tests that the Holocaust was ENABLED by wartime conditions: the chaos of occupation, the use of war as cover, the involvement of collaborators across occupied Europe; genocide studies show that most perpetrators were ordinary people following orders in conditions of dehumanization — Hannah Arendt's 'banality of evil'

title: Atomic Bombs and the End of Total War
objectives: Master Atomic Bombs and the End of Total War for the Global Conflict (c. 1900–present) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: unprecedented government-science collaboration driven by fear Germany would get the bomb first
immediate deaths 130,000-226,000; debate over whether invasion alternative would have cost more
mutual assured destruction preventing direct great-power conflict

traps: Treating the atomic bomb decision as obviously right or wrong — AP tests HISTORICAL CONTEXT: in August 1945, Japan had not offered unconditional surrender; Battle of Okinawa suggested invasion would cost 250,000+ American casualties; Truman decided with this information, not hindsight; AP wants analysis of decision-making context, not moral verdict

title: The Cold War — Origins and Ideology
objectives: Master The Cold War — Origins and Ideology for the Cold War and Decolonization (c. 1900–present) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: capitalism/democracy vs. communism/one-party state
Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, NATO as US strategy
security buffer, spreading communist revolution as defensive

traps: Presenting the Cold War as entirely American vs. Soviet — AP tests that BOTH sides had legitimate security concerns: Soviets lost 27 million in WWII and wanted buffer states; Americans feared communist expansion; treating one side as entirely aggressive misses the security dilemma dynamic that AP rewards in SAQ and LEQ responses

title: Decolonization — Africa and Asia
objectives: Master Decolonization — Africa and Asia for the Cold War and Decolonization (c. 1900–present) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: partition creating India and Pakistan along religious lines, causing 1 million deaths
mostly peaceful transfer but with notable violent exceptions (Algeria, Kenya)
violence as psychologically necessary for colonial liberation

traps: Treating decolonization as a gift from European powers — AP tests that it was FORCED by independence movements, post-WWII weakness of European states, and Cold War pressure (US and USSR both officially anti-colonial); Britain and France did not voluntarily relinquish empire; the pace and nature of independence was determined by the strength of resistance movements

title: Non-Aligned Movement and the Third World
objectives: Third World as a political identity, not just economic description

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Asian and African nations refusing to choose between US and Soviet blocs
leaders using Cold War competition to extract aid from both sides

traps: Treating non-alignment as weakness or fence-sitting — AP tests it as a STRATEGIC CHOICE that gave developing nations leverage: by threatening to align with the other side, non-aligned nations extracted aid, weapons, and political recognition from both superpowers; Nasser got the Aswan Dam funded by the USSR after the US withdrew; this was sophisticated power politics

title: China's Communist Revolution and Mao
objectives: Master China's Communist Revolution and Mao for the Cold War and Decolonization (c. 1900–present) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: peasant-based revolution (not urban proletariat)
collectivization causing 15-45 million deaths from famine
Red Guards attacking 'bourgeois' culture, intellectuals sent to re-education camps

traps: Treating Mao's policies as simply evil or misguided — AP tests that the Great Leap Forward was based on ideological beliefs about the superiority of will over expertise; local officials falsified grain production data and people starved while grain was exported; the famine resulted from ideology + political incentives to lie + information suppression — a systemic failure, not just individual cruelty

title: Cold War Proxy Conflicts — Korea, Vietnam, Angola
objectives: Proxy wars drawing Third World nations into superpower competition regardless of local causes

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: UN intervention freezing conflict at 38th parallel; still technically ongoing
US escalation based on domino theory; Tet Offensive turning American public opinion

traps: Treating proxy wars as caused by Cold War competition — AP tests LOCAL CAUSES: the Vietnamese conflict had its own anti-colonial logic predating US involvement; the Korean War was a civil war with deep domestic roots; Cold War competition intensified these conflicts but didn't create them; conflating Cold War causes with local causes loses points on DBQ

title: End of the Cold War — Soviet Collapse
objectives: Gorbachev's glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring) unintentionally unleashing nationalism

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Soviet command economy unable to compete with US consumer economy
Eastern European states choosing independence when Gorbachev refused to use military force

traps: Attributing Soviet collapse solely to US pressure (Reagan's military spending) — AP tests INTERNAL causes: Soviet economic stagnation, ethnic nationalism in republics, and Gorbachev's reform miscalculations were primary; US pressure was a contributing factor but the Soviet Union collapsed from internal contradictions; single-cause answers receive partial credit

title: Apartheid and Post-Colonial State Challenges
objectives: Mandela's release (1990) and Truth and Reconciliation Commission as alternative to retribution

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: racial segregation institutionalized by law; ANC resistance; international sanctions
artificial borders, ethnic conflict, economic dependency on former colonial powers

traps: Treating decolonization as solving colonialism's problems — AP tests CONTINUITIES: colonial-era borders ignoring ethnic distribution caused post-independence conflicts (Rwanda, Nigeria); export economies built for European consumption persisted after independence; neo-colonialism through multinational corporations and debt replaced formal colonialism

title: Women and Decolonization — Promises and Limits
objectives: Master Women and Decolonization — Promises and Limits for the Cold War and Decolonization (c. 1900–present) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Algeria (FLN), Vietnam, Kenya (Mau Mau)
nationalist leaders often reverting to patriarchal structures after gaining power
constitutions granting rights not translating to lived reality

traps: Treating women's participation in independence movements as leading automatically to equality — AP tests the PATTERN of post-independence rollback; Algerian women who fought the French were told to return to domestic roles after independence; this pattern appears across decolonization and AP tests whether students can identify the gap between revolutionary rhetoric and post-revolutionary practice

title: Economic Globalization — Free Trade and Its Critics
objectives: Master Economic Globalization — Free Trade and Its Critics for the Globalization (c. 1900–present) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: IMF and World Bank creating post-WWII economic order
IMF requiring privatization and austerity in exchange for loans
reducing tariffs expanding trade but increasing inequality within countries

traps: Treating globalization as purely beneficial or purely harmful — AP tests CONTESTED EFFECTS: GDP growth in developing nations but also increased inequality; Western consumers benefiting from cheap goods while factory workers in developing nations face unsafe conditions; a complete analysis identifies winners and losers at multiple scales (global, national, class)

title: Technology and Cultural Globalization
objectives: Internet enabling instantaneous global communication and commerce
American cultural exports (film, music, fast food) creating 'McDonaldization' critique

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: local cultures blending with global influences rather than being replaced

traps: Treating cultural globalization as simple American domination — AP tests HYBRIDITY and RESISTANCE: Bollywood producing more films than Hollywood; K-pop as non-Western global cultural export; local food traditions persisting alongside McDonald's; the AP rewards nuanced analysis that acknowledges both homogenization pressures and local adaptation

title: Climate Change and Environmental Globalization
objectives: Industrial emissions since 1850 driving atmospheric CO2 increase

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: individual rational behavior producing collective environmental harm
voluntary national commitments without enforcement mechanism

traps: Treating climate change as only a recent issue — AP tests HISTORICAL CAUSATION: industrial revolution beginning the carbon accumulation problem; deforestation for plantation agriculture (colonial period) contributing; the current crisis has a 200-year causal history that AP expects students to connect to earlier periods using continuity reasoning

title: Disease, Migration, and Global Health
objectives: Master Disease, Migration, and Global Health for the Globalization (c. 1900–present) unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: WWI mobilization spreading disease globally, killing 50-100 million
from regional disease to global pandemic through migration and trade networks
WHO coordinating international response to pandemic threats

traps: Treating pandemics as natural disasters without historical context — AP tests the HUMAN causes: WWI troop movements spread the 1918 flu; global trade routes carried HIV; colonialism disrupting ecosystems created conditions for zoonotic disease emergence; connecting pandemic history to political/economic systems is the AP-level analysis that earns top scores

title: Continuity and Change in the 21st Century
objectives: Terrorism and asymmetric warfare replacing state-on-state conflict
Rising China challenging US-led world order — echoes of earlier hegemonic transitions

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: wealth gap within and between nations wider than at any time since 1900

traps: Treating the present as entirely unprecedented — AP tests HISTORICAL PARALLELS: US-China tension mirrors UK-Germany tension before WWI (Thucydides Trap); inequality patterns echo Gilded Age; terrorist tactics echo anarchist violence of early 20th century; connecting current events to historical patterns is exactly the synthesis skill AP World History tests in the LEQ

title: Ecosystem Structure — Who Eats Whom and Why It Matters
objectives: Producers, consumers, decomposers — roles in energy and nutrient cycling

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: complexity and stability
removing a predator ripples through the web

traps: Describing food webs only as 'who eats what' — AP FRQ asks about CONSEQUENCES of removing a species; must trace effects through multiple trophic levels

title: Energy Flow and the 10% Rule
objectives: Only ~10% of energy transferred between trophic levels
Gross primary productivity (GPP) vs. net primary productivity (NPP)
Why terrestrial ecosystems have higher NPP than open ocean

sections.title: Energy Flow and the 10% Rule
traps: Applying the 10% rule to matter/nutrients — nutrients recycle, energy does not; the 10% rule is energy-only; confusing these on FRQ loses full credit

title: Biogeochemical Cycles — Carbon, Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Water
objectives: Master Biogeochemical Cycles — Carbon, Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Water for the The Living World: Ecosystems unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion, ocean buffering
fixation (N₂ → NH₃), nitrification, denitrification pathways
no atmospheric reservoir; slow weathering release

traps: Confusing nitrogen fixation with nitrification — fixation converts N₂ gas to usable NH₃ (only bacteria do this); nitrification converts NH₃ to NO₃⁻

title: Terrestrial Biomes — Climate Determines Structure
objectives: Temperature and precipitation as the two axes determining biome type
Latitude, altitude, and continentality effects on biome distribution

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: tropical rainforest, temperate deciduous, grassland, desert, tundra

traps: Memorizing biome lists without understanding the climate logic — AP gives a climate graph (climatograph) and asks you to identify the biome; must know precipitation seasonality patterns

title: Aquatic Biomes and Zones
objectives: Estuaries as highly productive transition zones

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: intertidal, photic, aphotic, benthic, pelagic
lakes (stratification, turnover), rivers, wetlands

traps: Forgetting that estuaries combine freshwater and marine inputs — AP tests why estuaries are so productive (nutrient input from both, shallow water, high light penetration)

title: Ecological Niches and Species Interactions
objectives: Competitive exclusion principle and niche partitioning as its resolution

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: what's possible vs. what's achieved
fitness effects on each partner

traps: Confusing fundamental (potential) with realized (actual) niche — competitive exclusion shrinks the realized niche; AP asks which is wider and why

title: Ecosystem Services — What Nature Provides
objectives: Provisioning, regulating, cultural, supporting services — categories and examples
Valuing ecosystem services economically for policy arguments

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: flood control, water purification, carbon storage

traps: Listing ecosystem services without connecting them to mechanisms — AP FRQ asks to explain HOW wetlands filter water (plant uptake, microbial processing of nutrients), not just that they do

title: Primary and Secondary Productivity Calculations
objectives: NPP = GPP - respiration; units in g C/m²/yr or kcal/m²/yr
Calculating energy available at each trophic level
Comparing productivity across biomes using data tables

sections.title: Primary and Secondary Productivity Calculations
traps: Using GPP instead of NPP for available energy — consumers can only use NPP (what's left after plant respiration); AP math FRQ always requires NPP as the starting value

title: Biodiversity — Three Levels and Why Each Matters
objectives: Genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity — distinct but interconnected
Why genetic diversity matters for disease resistance and adaptation

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: high endemism + high threat

traps: Treating biodiversity as just species count — AP distinguishes all three levels and asks which type is affected by a specific threat (inbreeding reduces genetic diversity; habitat loss reduces species diversity)

title: Evolution and Natural Selection as Biodiversity Engine
objectives: Adaptive radiation and why island/isolated environments accelerate it
Extinction vs. speciation rate determining net biodiversity

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: allopatric vs. sympatric

traps: Treating evolution as slow and irrelevant to current conservation — rapid evolution (antibiotic resistance, pesticide resistance) is a current AP topic

title: Island Biogeography — A Model for Habitat Patches
objectives: Immigration rate and extinction rate reaching equilibrium species number

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: larger islands have lower extinction rates
closer islands have higher immigration rates

traps: Not applying island biogeography to fragmented habitats — AP explicitly tests that forest fragments, parks, and reserves function as ecological islands

title: Threats to Biodiversity — HIPPO
objectives: Habitat destruction as #1 threat globally
Overexploitation, pollution, climate change as additional drivers

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: competitive, predatory, and disease mechanisms

traps: Ranking threats without supporting data — AP FRQ asks to justify which threat is greatest using specific evidence; 'habitat destruction' without mechanism loses points

title: Keystone Species and Trophic Cascades
objectives: Sea otter / sea urchin / kelp as the canonical AP case study

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: disproportionate impact relative to biomass
top predator removal increases herbivore, decreases vegetation

traps: Confusing keystone with apex predator — a keystone species has outsized community impact but isn't necessarily the top predator; starfish and sea otters are classic AP keystone examples

title: Conservation Strategies — Protected Areas and Corridors
objectives: Habitat corridors allowing gene flow between fragmented populations
Minimum viable population and extinction vortex

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: one large vs. several small reserves

traps: Assuming larger reserves are always better — AP tests nuances: multiple small reserves may cover more habitat types; edge effects reduce effective interior area of large reserves

title: Invasive Species — Mechanisms and Case Studies
objectives: Economic and ecological costs of invasive species

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: enemy release, novel weapons, phenotypic plasticity
zebra mussels, kudzu, cane toads, Asian carp

traps: Saying invasives succeed 'because they have no predators' — that's enemy release hypothesis, one explanation; AP may ask for multiple mechanisms or ask you to evaluate evidence

title: Endangered Species and International Agreements
objectives: Captive breeding and reintroduction programs — success factors

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: criteria for critically endangered vs. vulnerable
trade restrictions for threatened species

traps: Confusing CITES (trade) with ESA (domestic US protection) — AP tests which treaty applies to international vs. domestic species protection scenarios

title: Population Dynamics — Growth Models
objectives: Per capita growth rate changes with density under logistic model

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: unlimited resources, r = biotic potential
K as carrying capacity, growth slows near K

traps: Using exponential model when logistic applies — AP gives data showing slowing growth and asks which model fits; must recognize S-curve features in data, not just graphs

title: Population Density and Distribution Patterns
objectives: Clumped, uniform, and random distribution — causes of each
Density-dependent vs. density-independent limiting factors

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: mark-recapture, transects, quadrats

traps: Confusing density-dependent (disease, competition, predation — intensity increases with density) with density-independent (weather, natural disasters — occur regardless of density)

title: Age Structure Diagrams — Predicting the Future
objectives: How current age structure predicts future growth momentum

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: growing, stable, declining populations
proportion of working-age to non-working-age population

traps: Reading age pyramids as snapshots not predictors — a country with many young people will CONTINUE growing even if fertility drops to replacement level immediately (population momentum)

title: Human Population Growth — Demographic Transition
objectives: Total fertility rate (TFR) vs. replacement fertility (2.1)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: high birth+death → falling death → falling birth → stable
education, urbanization, women's rights

traps: Applying demographic transition uniformly to all countries — different countries are in different stages; AP gives TFR and death rate data and asks which stage and what policy would be effective

title: Survivorship Curves — Who Dies When
objectives: Type I (late loss — humans, elephants), Type II (constant — birds), Type III (early loss — fish, plants)
Connecting curve type to life history strategy (r vs. K selection)
Survivorship data interpretation from tables

sections.title: Survivorship Curves — Who Dies When
traps: Memorizing examples without understanding mechanism — AP asks WHY fish are Type III (massive egg production, minimal parental care, most die young) not just that they are Type III

title: Resource Consumption and Ecological Footprint
objectives: Per capita resource consumption differences between developed and developing nations

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: land area required to support a lifestyle
Impact = Population × Affluence × Technology

traps: Blaming only population size for environmental impact — AP tests IPAT; a small wealthy population can have more impact than a large poor population due to affluence factor

title: Sustainable Yield and Fisheries Management
objectives: ITQs and catch limits as management tools

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: harvesting at K/2 for fastest regrowth
individual incentive vs. collective optimum

traps: Thinking MSY means harvest as much as possible — MSY is at K/2 where population growth rate is maximum; overfishing past MSY depletes the population

title: Human Population Policies and Ethics
objectives: Pro-natalist vs. anti-natalist policies — when each is used
Education and access to family planning as most effective interventions

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: demographic consequences (sex ratio, aging)

traps: Evaluating policies only on effectiveness without ethical dimensions — AP FRQ often asks for both effectiveness AND tradeoffs/consequences; China's policy reduced growth but created aging crisis

title: Plate Tectonics and Earth's Interior
objectives: Convection in mantle driving plate movement
Earthquakes and volcanoes concentrated at plate boundaries

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: divergent, convergent, transform — landforms at each

traps: Confusing subduction (oceanic under continental or oceanic under oceanic) with collision (continental-continental) — AP asks which plate boundary creates which feature

title: The Rock Cycle and Soil Formation
objectives: Weathering (physical and chemical) as soil formation mechanism

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: formation and interconversion
O, A, B, C layers and what each contains

traps: Describing soil only by texture, not horizon — AP FRQ asks about which horizon is most fertile (A horizon) and why (accumulated organic matter from decomposition)

title: The Atmosphere — Structure and Composition
objectives: Troposphere contains weather; stratosphere contains ozone layer

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: properties of each
CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, H₂O vapor — relative forcing

traps: Treating ozone depletion and greenhouse effect as the same problem — ozone depletion is in the stratosphere from CFCs; greenhouse effect is in the troposphere from CO₂/CH₄; they're distinct

title: Solar Radiation, Albedo, and Earth's Energy Budget
objectives: Latitude effects on solar angle and energy intensity

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: fraction of solar radiation reflected; ice-albedo feedback
shortwave in, longwave out, greenhouse retention

traps: Confusing albedo with emissivity — albedo is about incoming shortwave; greenhouse effect involves outgoing longwave; ice-albedo feedback links melting ice to more warming

title: Global Wind Patterns and Ocean Currents
objectives: Coriolis effect deflecting winds and ocean currents

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: rising/falling air creating wind belts
density-driven global ocean conveyor

traps: Not connecting wind patterns to precipitation — air rises at equator (wet) and descends at 30° (desert belt); AP gives a location's latitude and asks about likely climate

title: El Niño/La Niña and Climate Variability
objectives: ENSO impacts on global precipitation patterns

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: weakened trade winds, warm water moves east, drought in Australia/Indonesia
strengthened trade winds, opposite effects of El Niño

traps: Confusing which region experiences drought vs. flooding — El Niño brings drought to western Pacific (Australia) and flooding to South America's west coast; AP tests specific regional effects

title: Water Systems — Hydrological Cycle and Freshwater
objectives: Master Water Systems — Hydrological Cycle and Freshwater for the Earth Systems and Resources unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff, infiltration
confined vs. unconfined; groundwater depletion
all water draining to a single outlet

traps: Ignoring groundwater when discussing freshwater — aquifers hold 30x more freshwater than all surface water; AP tests Ogallala Aquifer depletion as a case study

title: Natural Disasters — Frequency, Magnitude, Prediction
objectives: Master Natural Disasters — Frequency, Magnitude, Prediction for the Earth Systems and Resources unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Richter scale logarithmic nature, P and S waves
viscosity and silica content predicting explosiveness
formation conditions (warm water, moisture, low wind shear)

traps: Not applying logarithmic scale to earthquake magnitude — a magnitude 7 earthquake releases 31.6× more energy than magnitude 6; AP gives Richter data expecting this relationship

title: Agriculture — Green Revolution and Its Consequences
objectives: High-yield variety crops, synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, irrigation
Subsistence vs. industrial agriculture tradeoffs

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: food production increase; costs: soil degradation, water use, chemical runoff

traps: Treating the Green Revolution as purely positive — AP FRQ asks for both benefits AND environmental costs; must address nutrient runoff (eutrophication), soil salinization from irrigation

title: Soil Degradation — Erosion, Salinization, Desertification
objectives: Master Soil Degradation — Erosion, Salinization, Desertification for the Land and Water Use unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: rates accelerated by tillage and removal of cover

terms.term: Salinization from irrigation in arid regions
terms.def: salt accumulation
land degradation at dry-land margins from overuse

traps: Confusing salinization (salt buildup from irrigation) with acidification (pH drop from industrial pollution or acid rain) — they have different causes and remediation strategies

title: Sustainable Agriculture — Conservation Practices
objectives: Master Sustainable Agriculture — Conservation Practices for the Land and Water Use unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: physical erosion control
biological and chemical soil conservation
minimizing pesticide use

traps: Listing conservation practices without explaining mechanisms — AP asks WHY contour plowing reduces erosion (water follows contour lines, slowing runoff rather than channeling downhill)

title: Forestry — Logging Methods and Their Impacts
objectives: Master Forestry — Logging Methods and Their Impacts for the Land and Water Use unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: extent of disturbance and recovery
biodiversity and carbon storage differences
agriculture, logging, urbanization

traps: Treating selective cutting as environmentally neutral — still causes soil compaction, erosion, edge effects, and fragmentation; AP asks you to compare specific environmental impacts of each method

title: Mining — Extraction Methods and Remediation
objectives: Surface mining (strip, open-pit) vs. subsurface mining — impact comparison

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: iron sulfide oxidation producing sulfuric acid
legal standards for post-mining restoration

traps: Describing mining impacts generally — AP expects specific chemistry: acid mine drainage involves FeS₂ + O₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ + Fe(OH)₃; must name the process and product

title: Fisheries and Aquaculture
objectives: Master Fisheries and Aquaculture for the Land and Water Use unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: declining catch per unit effort, smaller fish
non-target species in commercial fishing nets
disease, escaped species, nutrient pollution

traps: Treating aquaculture as a sustainable solution without caveats — AP FRQ asks for problems with aquaculture (water pollution from waste, disease spread, escaped fish competing with wild stocks)

title: Urban Land Use and Sprawl
objectives: Master Urban Land Use and Sprawl for the Land and Water Use unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: dark surfaces, reduced vegetation
increased stormwater runoff and reduced groundwater recharge
density, transit, green space

traps: Explaining urban heat islands only by human heat generation — dark surfaces absorbing more radiation and evapotranspiration loss (no vegetation) are the main mechanisms; human waste heat is secondary

title: Water Use, Diversion, and Irrigation Issues
objectives: Master Water Use, Diversion, and Irrigation Issues for the Land and Water Use unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: efficiency comparison
diversion leading to ecosystem collapse
prior appropriation vs. riparian rights

traps: Not quantifying water use differences — drip irrigation uses 30-50% less water than flood; AP gives efficiency data and asks to calculate water savings or evaluate policy options

title: Fossil Fuels — Formation, Extraction, Environmental Costs
objectives: EROI (Energy Return on Energy Investment) declining for fossil fuels

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: relative carbon content and emissions per unit energy
surface mining, fracking, deep-sea drilling — environmental risks of each

traps: Ranking fossil fuels only by CO₂ without considering other pollutants — coal produces most CO₂ AND SO₂/NOx/particulates; natural gas burns cleaner but has methane leakage issues

title: Nuclear Energy — Fission, Waste, and Risk
objectives: Master Nuclear Energy — Fission, Waste, and Risk for the Energy Resources and Consumption unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: U-235 splits releasing neutrons and energy
half-life and long-term storage challenges
what went wrong and why containment matters

traps: Treating nuclear as either zero-risk or too dangerous without nuance — AP FRQ asks for specific advantages (no CO₂ emissions, high energy density) AND disadvantages (waste storage, accident risk)

title: Solar Energy — Photovoltaic and Passive Systems
objectives: Intermittency problem and storage solutions

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: semiconductor converting photons to electrons
orientation, thermal mass, glazing

traps: Ignoring lifecycle environmental costs of solar — manufacturing solar panels requires mining rare earth elements and produces toxic waste; AP tests full lifecycle analysis

title: Wind, Hydro, and Geothermal Energy
objectives: Master Wind, Hydro, and Geothermal Energy for the Energy Resources and Consumption unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: capacity factor (~30%), bird/bat mortality, visual impact
reliable but habitat disruption, altered sediment flow
limited to tectonically active regions, H₂S emissions

traps: Treating all renewables as equally applicable everywhere — hydroelectric requires significant elevation drop and water flow; geothermal requires volcanic activity; AP tests location-specific feasibility

title: Biofuels and Biomass Energy
objectives: First generation (food crops) vs. second generation (cellulosic) biofuels

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: EROI for corn ethanol is near 1
food vs. fuel vs. forest

traps: Assuming biofuels are carbon-neutral — only if regrowth absorbs all CO₂ emitted; corn ethanol lifecycle often produces more GHG than gasoline when land use change is included

title: Energy Conservation and Efficiency
objectives: First law (quantity) vs. second law (quality) efficiency losses

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: using waste heat to increase overall efficiency
insulation, HVAC, lighting efficiency improvements

traps: Confusing efficiency with conservation — efficiency means getting more output per unit energy input; conservation means using less total energy; AP asks for both strategies

title: The Energy Mix — Global and US Patterns
objectives: Percentage contributions of fossil fuels, nuclear, renewables globally and in US
Electricity grid vs. transportation sector energy sources
Energy security and geopolitical implications of fossil fuel dependence

sections.title: The Energy Mix — Global and US Patterns
traps: Giving outdated energy mix percentages — AP provides current data tables; must read the given data rather than relying on memorized percentages from different years

title: Energy Policy — Economics, Subsidies, and Incentives
objectives: Fossil fuel subsidies vs. renewable energy incentives
Cost-benefit analysis of energy transition

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: mechanisms and tradeoffs

traps: Describing policy without mechanism — AP FRQ asks HOW a carbon tax reduces emissions (raises price → reduces demand/shifts to alternatives), not just that it does

title: Air Pollutants — Primary and Secondary
