objectives: EPA six criteria pollutants and their health effects

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: emitted directly (SO₂, NOx, CO, particulates, VOCs)
formed in atmosphere (ozone, PAN, H₂SO₄, HNO₃)

traps: Confusing ground-level ozone (bad, tropospheric pollutant) with stratospheric ozone (good, UV shield) — AP explicitly tests this distinction; the same molecule has opposite effects at different altitudes

title: Photochemical Smog Formation
objectives: NOx + VOCs + sunlight → ozone + PAN (photochemical smog)
Temperature inversion trapping pollutants near surface

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: cars + sunlight + topography creating smog

traps: Confusing photochemical smog (ozone-based, sunny cities) with industrial/London smog (sulfurous, foggy, cold) — different chemistry, different conditions, different health effects

title: Acid Deposition — Chemistry and Ecological Damage
objectives: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ → H₂SO₄; NOx + H₂O → HNO₃

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: aluminum mobilization at pH < 5
acid rain affecting regions far from sources

traps: Treating acid rain as only a local problem — emissions in Ohio create acid rain in New England due to prevailing westerly winds; AP tests transboundary pollution and international policy

title: Stratospheric Ozone Depletion
objectives: Montreal Protocol as policy success story

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Cl + O₃ → ClO + O₂; ClO + O → Cl + O₂ (Cl regenerated)
polar stratospheric clouds concentrating Cl

traps: Saying CFCs 'destroy' ozone as a one-time reaction — each Cl atom catalytically destroys ~100,000 ozone molecules before being removed; the catalytic cycle is the critical AP concept

title: Indoor Air Pollution
objectives: VOCs from building materials and cleaning products
Developing world indoor air pollution from biomass combustion

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: natural radioactive gas from uranium decay, lung cancer risk

traps: Overlooking indoor air quality as an AP topic — AP specifically tests radon (enter through foundation cracks, accumulates in basements) and its mechanism of harm (alpha particle emission in lungs)

title: The Clean Air Act and Pollution Reduction
objectives: NAAQS standards for six criteria pollutants
Best available control technology (BACT) requirements
Cap-and-trade for SO₂ under 1990 CAA Amendments

sections.title: The Clean Air Act and Pollution Reduction
traps: Treating regulation as binary (yes/no) — AP tests HOW regulations work; cap-and-trade sets total emissions cap, issues permits, allows trading so cheapest reductions happen first

title: Noise and Light Pollution
objectives: Master Noise and Light Pollution for the Atmospheric Pollution unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: disrupted communication, navigation, reproduction
disrupted circadian rhythms, sea turtle disorientation
shielding lights, reducing unnecessary illumination

traps: Treating noise/light pollution as trivial AP topics — they appear in FRQ expecting mechanistic explanations; sea turtles navigate by moon over ocean, artificial lights cause disorientation

title: Climate Change and Atmospheric Pollution Linkages
objectives: Black carbon (soot) both absorbs radiation AND causes health problems
Ozone as both pollutant (troposphere) and greenhouse gas

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: improving air quality AND reducing warming

traps: Separating air pollution from climate policy — methane reduction prevents climate change AND reduces ground-level ozone; AP tests these co-benefits

title: Water Pollution — Point vs. Nonpoint Sources
objectives: Master Water Pollution — Point vs. Nonpoint Sources for the Aquatic and Terrestrial Pollution unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: specific location (pipe, drain) — easier to regulate
diffuse (agricultural runoff, urban stormwater) — harder to control
discharge permits for point sources

traps: Applying point source regulations to nonpoint problems — a farmer's field has no single discharge point; AP tests why nonpoint source pollution is harder to regulate and what strategies address it

title: Eutrophication — Nutrient Pollution Mechanisms
objectives: Nitrogen and phosphorus runoff → algal bloom → decomposition → oxygen depletion

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Gulf of Mexico as primary AP case study
adding phosphorus to freshwater triggers growth

traps: Confusing which nutrient limits which system — phosphorus usually limits freshwater systems; nitrogen usually limits marine/coastal systems; AP asks about the specific system in the scenario

title: Toxic Pollutants and Biomagnification
objectives: Bioaccumulation in individual organisms vs. biomagnification across food web

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: concentration increases at higher trophic levels
fat-soluble or non-metabolizable, concentrate in fatty tissue

traps: Confusing bioaccumulation (within one organism over time) with biomagnification (increasing concentration across trophic levels) — AP explicitly distinguishes these two processes

title: Solid Waste — Types, Disposal, Reduction
objectives: Master Solid Waste — Types, Disposal, Reduction for the Aquatic and Terrestrial Pollution unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: food (most by weight), paper, plastics
liner, leachate collection, methane capture
reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose

traps: Treating recycling as the top priority — the waste hierarchy puts REDUCTION first; AP FRQ asks to rank strategies and explain why source reduction is more effective than recycling

title: Hazardous Waste — Classification and Superfund
objectives: Master Hazardous Waste — Classification and Superfund for the Aquatic and Terrestrial Pollution unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity, toxicity
polluter-pays principle, National Priorities List
contaminated industrial sites and redevelopment challenges

traps: Assuming all industrial waste is regulated the same — RCRA governs current hazardous waste; CERCLA (Superfund) addresses historical abandoned sites; AP tests which law applies to which scenario

title: Oil Spills — Impacts and Remediation
objectives: Master Oil Spills — Impacts and Remediation for the Aquatic and Terrestrial Pollution unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: coating seabirds, smothering benthic organisms
PAH compounds affecting fish reproduction
hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria as cleanup tool

traps: Focusing only on visible oil effects — long-term chronic effects from PAH compounds and dispersant toxicity persist for decades; AP tests both acute and long-term impacts of spills

title: Soil Contamination and Remediation
objectives: In-situ vs. ex-situ remediation tradeoffs

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: lead, arsenic, cadmium from mining/industry
plants (hyperaccumulators) extracting metals from soil

traps: Describing phytoremediation without mechanism — plants must be harvested AND disposed of properly to actually remove metals from the site; if left to decompose, metals return to soil

title: Environmental Justice — Pollution Burden Distribution
objectives: Disproportionate pollution exposure in low-income and minority communities
Locally unwanted land uses (LULUs) and siting decisions
EJ movement and EPA environmental justice policies

sections.title: Environmental Justice — Pollution Burden Distribution
traps: Treating environmental justice as separate from environmental science — AP FRQ integrates EJ with pollution topics; must connect which communities bear the greatest burden from specific pollutants

title: The Greenhouse Effect and Climate Science
objectives: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, H₂O as greenhouse gases — relative warming potential

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: shortwave in, longwave absorbed by GHGs, re-radiated toward Earth
ice cores, temperature records, sea level rise, Arctic sea ice

traps: Explaining climate change vaguely — AP FRQ requires molecular mechanism: greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared radiation because their bonds vibrate at IR frequencies

title: Climate Feedbacks — Amplifying and Dampening
objectives: Master Climate Feedbacks — Amplifying and Dampening for the Global Change unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: ice-albedo, water vapor amplification, permafrost methane
blackbody radiation, cloud albedo effects
threshold beyond which feedbacks become self-sustaining

traps: Calling all climate feedbacks positive (amplifying) — negative feedbacks also exist; AP tests that more outgoing radiation as temperature rises is a stabilizing (negative) feedback

title: Climate Change Impacts — Ecological and Human
objectives: Master Climate Change Impacts — Ecological and Human for the Global Change unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: earlier spring events disrupting predator-prey timing
thermal expansion + ice melt; coastal flooding
thermal stress expelling zooxanthellae

traps: Listing impacts without connecting to mechanism — coral bleaching: warmer water stresses zooxanthellae (symbiotic algae), coral expels them (bleaches), loses food source and may die if prolonged

title: Ocean Acidification
objectives: pH drop dissolving calcium carbonate shells of marine organisms
Pteropods, oysters, corals as most vulnerable organisms

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: chemistry of acidification

traps: Confusing ocean acidification with general ocean pollution — caused specifically by dissolved CO₂ from atmosphere; pH has dropped from 8.2 to 8.1 (30% more acidic); AP tests the chemistry

title: Mitigation Strategies — Reducing Emissions
objectives: Renewable energy transition, electrification of transportation

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: geological sequestration
reforestation, soil carbon, methane capture from landfills

traps: Treating mitigation as only energy-sector solutions — AP tests agriculture (methane, N₂O from fertilizer), land use change, and waste sector contributions to total GHG inventory

title: Adaptation Strategies — Living With Climate Change
objectives: Sea walls, managed retreat, living shorelines for coastal flooding
Heat-resilient crops and shifting agricultural zones
Early warning systems and disaster preparedness

sections.title: Adaptation Strategies — Living With Climate Change
traps: Confusing mitigation (preventing emissions) with adaptation (adjusting to changes) — AP FRQ distinguishes and asks which strategy addresses a specific scenario

title: International Climate Policy — UNFCCC, Paris Agreement
objectives: Carbon markets and international emissions trading

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: NDCs, 1.5°C and 2°C targets, review mechanism
developed vs. developing nations

traps: Treating the Paris Agreement as legally binding — it's a voluntary pledge system (NDCs); lack of enforcement mechanism is a key weakness; AP asks about both structure and limitations

title: Ozone Recovery and Environmental Policy Lessons
objectives: Using Montreal Protocol as model for climate policy discussions

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: phaseout of CFCs leading to measurable ozone recovery
HCFCs → HFCs (some still potent GHGs)

traps: Treating ozone recovery as complete — the ozone hole still forms annually but is smaller than peak; full recovery projected for 2060s; AP tests that HFC replacements became a new climate problem

title: Constitutional Foundations — Compromises and Design
objectives: Master Constitutional Foundations — Compromises and Design for the Foundations of American Democracy unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: dividing sovereignty between national and state governments

terms.term: Separation of powers with checks and balances
terms.def: each branch limiting the others
Declaration, Constitution, Federalist 10, Federalist 51, Brutus 1

traps: Summarizing the Federalist Papers without using specific arguments — AP requires SPECIFIC arguments from specific documents: Federalist 10 argues large republic REDUCES faction influence (extended sphere argument); Federalist 51 argues ambition counteracting ambition through separated powers; Brutus 1 argues large republic makes representatives too distant and government too powerful; free response requires applying these specific arguments to modern scenarios

title: Federalism — Division and Evolution
objectives: Enumerated powers (Article I §8) vs. implied powers (necessary and proper clause)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: expanding federal power through implied powers and supremacy
federal grants-in-aid creating interdependence, blurring boundaries

traps: Treating federalism as a fixed division of power — AP tests that federalism is CONTESTED and EVOLVING; McCulloch expanded federal power; New Deal further expanded it; Reagan tried to reduce it; the current system (cooperative federalism) uses grants with conditions to influence state behavior without direct mandates; AP free response asks how specific events or court cases CHANGED the federal balance

title: Civil Liberties — First Amendment and Its Limits
objectives: Master Civil Liberties — First Amendment and Its Limits for the Foundations of American Democracy unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: 14th Amendment applying Bill of Rights to states (Gitlow, McDonald)
speech, press, religion, assembly, petition — each with different judicial tests

terms.term: Schenck 'clear and present danger' → Brandenburg test
terms.def: imminent lawless action required for speech restriction

traps: Treating First Amendment as absolute — AP tests LIMITS: obscenity (Miller test), fighting words, imminent lawless incitement are NOT protected; prior restraint is almost never allowed (Near v. Minnesota) but national security exceptions exist; AP free response frequently presents a First Amendment scenario and asks you to apply the correct judicial test, not just state that free speech exists

title: Civil Rights — Equal Protection and Its Evolution
objectives: Strict scrutiny (race, national origin), intermediate scrutiny (sex), rational basis (economic)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: basis for civil rights litigation
Brown v. Board, Engel v. Vitale, Schenck, Tinker, Gideon, Miranda, Roe, McDonald, Citizens United

traps: Knowing the case holdings without knowing WHY they are required — AP specifically lists 15 required Supreme Court cases; you must know the CONSTITUTIONAL QUESTION, the HOLDING, and the REASONING; for free response, cases must be applied to new scenarios; Brown matters not just as a fact (segregation unconstitutional) but as reasoning (psychological harm + 14th Amendment equal protection); apply the reasoning, not just the outcome

title: Congress — Structure, Powers, and Lawmaking
objectives: Master Congress — Structure, Powers, and Lawmaking for the Interactions Among Branches of Government unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: House represents population; Senate represents states — different constituencies
where most legislation lives and dies; chairs having gatekeeping power
Senate unlimited debate requiring 60 votes (cloture) to end — minority veto power

traps: Treating the filibuster as constitutional — it is a SENATE RULE, not in the Constitution; AP tests the distinction between constitutional requirements (Article I) and procedural rules (Senate standing rules); the filibuster can be changed by Senate rule change (nuclear option); AP frequently tests why Congress is 'inefficient' — the answer is procedural obstacles (filibuster, committee gatekeeping) plus electoral incentives, not constitutional design alone

title: The Presidency — Formal and Informal Powers
objectives: Master The Presidency — Formal and Informal Powers for the Interactions Among Branches of Government unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: veto, commander-in-chief, appointment, treaty, State of the Union
executive orders, signing statements, executive privilege, bully pulpit
requiring congressional notification within 48 hours — presidents have ignored it

traps: Treating executive orders as equivalent to laws — executive orders are ADMINISTRATIVE directives that can be overturned by the next president or struck down by courts; they are not laws requiring congressional passage; AP tests that presidents use executive orders precisely BECAUSE Congress won't act; the political debate about executive overreach is testable as a checks and balances question

title: The Federal Bureaucracy — Implementation and Accountability
objectives: Master The Federal Bureaucracy — Implementation and Accountability for the Interactions Among Branches of Government unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: bureaucratic agency + congressional committee + interest group forming mutually beneficial relationship
quasi-legislative (rules) and quasi-judicial (adjudication) functions
hearings, budget control, confirmation power limiting bureaucratic independence

traps: Treating the bureaucracy as simply implementing laws — AP tests DISCRETION: bureaucrats make policy choices through rule-making and enforcement priorities; the EPA choosing which industries to audit is a policy decision; the iron triangle shows that bureaucracies develop political allies that make them hard to control; AP free response asks how Congress or the President can control bureaucratic behavior — know specific oversight mechanisms

title: Federal Courts — Structure, Selection, and Judicial Review
objectives: Master Federal Courts — Structure, Selection, and Judicial Review for the Interactions Among Branches of Government unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Marbury v. Madison establishing courts' power to strike down unconstitutional laws
presidential nomination + Senate confirmation — making courts politically contested
debate over appropriate scope of judicial power

traps: Treating judicial review as explicitly in the Constitution — it is NOT; Marshall CLAIMED this power in Marbury v. Madison; AP tests the political nature of judicial selection (presidents appointing ideologically compatible justices) and the legitimacy debate (unelected judges invalidating democratic laws); free response asks you to evaluate competing perspectives on judicial power using specific cases and arguments

title: Selective Incorporation — Applying Rights to States
objectives: Master Selective Incorporation — Applying Rights to States for the Civil Liberties and Civil Rights unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Bill of Rights originally applied only to federal government
vehicle for incorporating rights against states
Second Amendment incorporated — states cannot ban handguns

traps: Assuming all rights are equally incorporated — NOT all Bill of Rights provisions are incorporated; the Third Amendment (quartering soldiers) has never been directly incorporated; AP tests which rights HAVE been incorporated through specific cases; the pattern is that fundamental rights get incorporated but some procedural rights (grand jury for state felonies) have not been; the free response may ask you to trace the incorporation of a specific right

title: Political Socialization and Public Opinion
objectives: Education, peers, media, religion as secondary socialization agents

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: party identification passed intergenerationally
sampling method determining validity (random sample vs. convenience sample)

traps: Treating public opinion as a fixed reflection of preferences — AP tests that opinion is CONSTRUCTED and MANIPULATED: question wording affects responses; polling methodology affects results; media framing shapes opinion; politicians use public opinion strategically while also responding to it; the relationship is interactive (politicians lead opinion AND follow it) rather than one-directional

title: Political Parties — Functions and Realignment
objectives: Two-party system reinforced by plurality voting (Duverger's Law) and ballot access laws

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: nomination, voter mobilization, organizing government, policy development
critical elections shifting party coalitions (1932, 1968)

traps: Treating party platforms as binding on elected officials — AP tests that the United States has WEAK parties compared to parliamentary systems; individual members vote against the party regularly; party identification is the strongest predictor of vote choice but doesn't control behavior; the difference between a party system that controls legislators (parliamentary) and one that loosely organizes them (US) is a key AP comparative government connection

title: Interest Groups and Campaign Finance
objectives: Master Interest Groups and Campaign Finance for the Political Participation unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Citizens United allowing unlimited independent expenditures
providing information and campaign contributions as primary influence mechanisms
iron triangles are stable; issue networks are fluid, open to more groups

traps: Treating all interest group activity as corruption — AP tests that interest groups perform LEGITIMATE democratic functions (aggregating preferences, providing information to legislators, mobilizing voters) alongside their problematic role in distorting policy toward concentrated interests; Citizens United is specifically tested: connecting spending to First Amendment (speech) and explaining why corporations can spend without disclosure limits

title: Elections and Voting Behavior
objectives: Master Elections and Voting Behavior for the Political Participation unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: winner-take-all in most states creating battleground state focus
name recognition, franking privilege, constituency service, fundraising
party ID strongest, then candidate image, then issues

traps: Treating voter choice as primarily about policy issues — AP tests that PARTY IDENTIFICATION is the strongest predictor of vote choice, not issue positions; most voters don't follow issues closely; candidate image (likability, leadership qualities) is second; specific issue positions matter primarily to high-information voters and swing voters; this evidence-based understanding of voting behavior requires applying political science research, not assumptions about rational voting

title: SOAPS and Context
objectives: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject
Exigence
Constraints

sections.title: SOAPS and Context
traps: Exigence = the urgency or problem that prompted the text; students often confuse it with purpose — exigence is WHY it was written NOW, purpose is WHAT the writer wants to achieve.

title: Audience and Register
objectives: Intended vs. unintended audience
Formal vs. informal register
Tone and audience relationship

sections.title: Audience and Register
traps: FRQ 2 (Rhetorical Analysis) always asks HOW choices affect the audience — never just label a device; explain the effect on the specific audience in context.

title: Purpose and Claim
objectives: Informative, persuasive, narrative purposes
Thesis vs. claim
Implicit vs. explicit purpose

sections.title: Purpose and Claim
traps: A complex thesis acknowledges complexity or tension — 'while X, Y because Z' scores higher than a simple assertion; practice writing nuanced claims, not just pro/con.

title: Types of Claims
objectives: Claims of fact, value, and policy
Thesis development
Arguable vs. factual claims

sections.title: Types of Claims
traps: Claims of policy argue 'should' — these require evidence for both the problem AND the solution; FRQ 3 (Argument) is almost always a policy claim.

title: Evidence Selection and Integration
objectives: Anecdotal, statistical, and testimonial evidence
Embedding quotations
Source credibility

sections.title: Evidence Selection and Integration
traps: Evidence alone earns no points — commentary explaining HOW the evidence supports your claim is what differentiates a 4 from a 6 on the argument FRQ.

title: Counterargument and Concession
objectives: Acknowledging opposing views
Concession-refutation structure
Straw man fallacy

sections.title: Counterargument and Concession
traps: Acknowledging a counterargument and then refuting or qualifying it shows sophistication — the 'complexity' point on the rubric requires engaging with tension, not ignoring it.

title: Logical Fallacies
objectives: Ad hominem, false dichotomy, slippery slope
Hasty generalization
Appeal to tradition

sections.title: Logical Fallacies
traps: MCQ passages often contain deliberate fallacies — identify the specific name and explain why it undermines the argument's logic, not just 'it's wrong'.

title: Ethos: Credibility and Trust
objectives: Establishing credibility
Shared values
Acknowledging limitations

sections.title: Ethos: Credibility and Trust
traps: Ethos isn't just about credentials — a writer builds ethos by conceding points fairly, using precise language, and demonstrating knowledge; look for all three in FRQ passages.

title: Logos: Logic and Evidence
objectives: Inductive vs. deductive reasoning
Analogical reasoning
Data and statistics

sections.title: Logos: Logic and Evidence
traps: Logos questions ask about the STRUCTURE of the argument — inductive (specific → general) vs. deductive (general → specific); deductive is stronger if the premises are accepted.

title: Pathos: Emotional Connection
objectives: Narrative and anecdote
Vivid diction and imagery
Shared values appeals

sections.title: Pathos: Emotional Connection
traps: Pathos is NOT manipulation — it becomes manipulative only when it substitutes for evidence; in rhetorical analysis, explain which emotion is triggered and why it's effective here.

title: Kairos and Timeliness
objectives: Right moment for argument
Cultural context
Exigence connection

sections.title: Kairos and Timeliness
traps: Kairos = the opportune moment — King's 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' has high kairos because it responds directly to a published letter of criticism; timeliness strengthens ethos.

title: Syntax and Sentence Structure
objectives: Periodic vs. cumulative sentences
Parallelism and anaphora
Fragments for effect

sections.title: Syntax and Sentence Structure
traps: Periodic sentence withholds the main clause until the end (creates suspense); cumulative adds details after main clause (builds picture) — both appear on MCQ with effect questions.

title: Diction and Tone
objectives: Connotation vs. denotation
Abstract vs. concrete diction
Shifts in tone

sections.title: Diction and Tone
traps: Tone shift questions: identify the before-tone, after-tone, and the turning word/phrase that signals the shift — 'yet', 'however', 'but' often mark the pivot.

title: Figurative Language
objectives: Metaphor and extended metaphor
Irony and satire
Hyperbole and understatement

sections.title: Figurative Language
traps: FRQ rhetorical analysis rarely rewards just naming 'metaphor' — explain what is being compared and how the comparison advances the author's argument or characterization.

title: Voice and Persona
objectives: Authorial voice vs. persona
Formal vs. colloquial voice
Reliability of narrators

sections.title: Voice and Persona
traps: In synthesis and argument FRQs, your own voice matters — avoid passive constructions and hedging language like 'it could be argued'; be direct and assertive in your prose.

title: Reading and Annotating Sources
objectives: Identifying source bias
Cross-referencing sources
Noting point of view

sections.title: Reading and Annotating Sources
traps: Synthesis FRQ requires using AT LEAST 3 of 6–7 provided sources — cite as (Source A) or (Source B); using 4+ sources distinguishes a 5 from a 6.

title: Building a Synthesis Argument
objectives: Developing a central claim
Integrating sources into your argument
Avoiding summary

sections.title: Building a Synthesis Argument
traps: The most common synthesis mistake: summarizing each source in a separate paragraph instead of weaving them into your own argument — sources should support YOU, not the other way around.

title: Citation and Attribution
objectives: In-text citation conventions
Attributing vs. citing
Avoiding plagiarism

sections.title: Citation and Attribution
traps: You do NOT use MLA/APA format on the AP exam — simply write '(Source C)' or 'as the graph in Source D shows'; no bibliography required.

title: Crafting the Argument Essay
objectives: Thesis with defensible claim
Line of reasoning
Evidence + commentary structure

sections.title: Crafting the Argument Essay
traps: The argument FRQ prompt gives you a statement to defend, challenge, or qualify — 'qualify' (agree with conditions) is the most sophisticated position and scores highest.

title: Organization and Transitions
objectives: Body paragraph structure
Transitional logic
Coherence at essay level

sections.title: Organization and Transitions
traps: Each body paragraph needs its own mini-claim (not just a topic sentence) that connects back to the thesis — a paragraph about evidence with no claim earns no reasoning points.

title: Revision and Editing Strategies
objectives: Recognizing wordiness
Strengthening weak claims
Checking evidence integration

sections.title: Revision and Editing Strategies
traps: MCQ grammar questions: eliminate passive voice, vague pronouns, and dangling modifiers — these are the three most tested editing issues on the multiple-choice section.

title: Maps and Spatial Thinking
objectives: Reference maps vs. thematic maps
Isoline maps
Choropleth maps

sections.title: Maps and Spatial Thinking
traps: Distinguish choropleth (shaded areas) from dot-density (individual dots) — FRQs ask you to justify which map type suits the data.

title: Geographic Data and GIS
objectives: GIS layers
Remote sensing
GPS applications

sections.title: Geographic Data and GIS
traps: GIS questions ask what you can COMBINE — overlay population, elevation, and land use; know that GPS is collection, GIS is analysis.

title: Scale and Region
objectives: Formal, functional, and vernacular regions
Scale of analysis
Geographic scale effects

sections.title: Scale and Region
traps: Vernacular/perceptual regions (like 'the South') are defined by perception, not data — students confuse these with formal regions.

title: Space, Place, and Landscape
objectives: Sense of place vs. space
Cultural landscape
Built environment

sections.title: Space, Place, and Landscape
traps: Cultural landscape = the visible imprint of culture on land; Sequent Occupance describes layers of successive cultures — know both terms with examples.

title: Models of Spatial Interaction
objectives: Gravity model
Distance decay
Space-time compression

sections.title: Models of Spatial Interaction
traps: Gravity model: interaction ∝ (Pop₁ × Pop₂) / Distance² — larger cities pull more; increasing distance reduces interaction exponentially.

title: Population Distribution and Density
objectives: Arithmetic vs. physiological density
Ecumene
Population clusters

sections.title: Population Distribution and Density
traps: Physiological density = population / arable land — higher than arithmetic in Egypt (most land is desert); always specify which density.

title: Demographic Transition Model
objectives: Stages 1–5
CBR, CDR, NIR
Stage 5 population decline

sections.title: Demographic Transition Model
traps: Stage 5 (sub-replacement fertility) is NOT on all versions of the DTM — know that Japan and Germany are examples; NIR < 0 in Stage 5.

title: Population Pyramids and Structure
objectives: Age-sex pyramids
Dependency ratio
Youth vs. elderly bulges

sections.title: Population Pyramids and Structure
traps: Wide base = Stage 2/3 (high youth, high future growth); narrow base = Stage 4/5 (aging population, strain on social services).

title: Malthus, Boserup, and Population Theory
objectives: Malthusian limits
Boserupian innovation
Neo-Malthusianism

sections.title: Malthus, Boserup, and Population Theory
traps: Malthus said population outruns food (pessimist); Boserup said necessity drives agricultural innovation (optimist) — FRQs ask you to apply both to a scenario.

title: Migration Push and Pull Factors
objectives: Ravenstein's laws
Push-pull model
Intervening obstacles

sections.title: Migration Push and Pull Factors
traps: Intervening opportunity (better option found en route) vs. intervening obstacle (barrier that stops migration) — students mix these up constantly.

title: Types of Migration
objectives: Voluntary vs. forced migration
Transhumance and cyclic movement
Refugees vs. IDPs

sections.title: Types of Migration
traps: Refugees cross international borders; IDPs (Internally Displaced Persons) stay within their country — this distinction matters for FRQ scoring.

title: Migration Patterns and Consequences
objectives: Brain drain
Remittances
Chain migration

sections.title: Migration Patterns and Consequences
traps: Remittances can exceed foreign aid in developing nations — brain drain and remittances are two sides of the same migration coin.

title: Cultural Traits, Complexes, and Regions
objectives: Material vs. nonmaterial culture
Culture complex
Cultural hearth

sections.title: Cultural Traits, Complexes, and Regions
traps: Cultural hearths are origin points of innovation (Mesopotamia, Nile Valley, Indus Valley) — distinguish hearth from cultural diffusion pathway.

title: Cultural Diffusion
objectives: Relocation diffusion
Expansion diffusion (contagious, hierarchical, stimulus)
Reverse hierarchical

sections.title: Cultural Diffusion
traps: Contagious = spreads like a disease (contact); Hierarchical = jumps city-to-city; Stimulus = idea adopts but adapts (McDonald's goes local) — know all four.

title: Language Distribution
objectives: Language families and branches
Lingua franca
Language extinction

sections.title: Language Distribution
traps: Indo-European is the largest family; within it, Romance vs. Germanic vs. Slavic branches — Swahili is an example of a lingua franca, not a family.

title: Religion and Sacred Space
objectives: Universalizing vs. ethnic religions
Sacred spaces
Religious landscapes

sections.title: Religion and Sacred Space
traps: Universalizing religions (Christianity, Islam, Buddhism) actively seek converts; Ethnic religions (Judaism, Hinduism) are tied to place/ethnicity — this is a key MCQ distinction.

title: Ethnicity, Race, and Cultural Identity
objectives: Ethnic enclaves
Multiculturalism vs. assimilation
Cultural identity and conflict

sections.title: Ethnicity, Race, and Cultural Identity
traps: Ethnic enclaves preserve culture (Little Italy, Chinatown) — distinguish from ghettos (forced segregation); FRQs ask you to identify which and explain why.

title: Gender and Cultural Norms
objectives: Gender roles across cultures
Female empowerment index
Gendered spaces

sections.title: Gender and Cultural Norms
traps: Gender inequality index and female education rates appear in development-themed FRQs — connect to DTM Stage and fertility rate.

title: Political Geography Concepts
objectives: Nation vs. state vs. nation-state
Stateless nations
Multi-state nations

sections.title: Political Geography Concepts
traps: The Kurds are the classic stateless nation example; the Arab nation spans multiple states — don't confuse 'state' (political unit) with 'nation' (cultural group).

title: Borders and Boundaries
objectives: Geometric vs. natural boundaries
Antecedent, subsequent, superimposed boundaries
Relic boundaries

sections.title: Borders and Boundaries
traps: Superimposed boundaries were drawn by outside powers ignoring cultural groups (Africa's colonial borders) — this is the root cause of many African conflicts.

title: Shape and Size of States
objectives: Compact, elongated, fragmented, prorupted, perforated states
Enclave vs. exclave

sections.title: Shape and Size of States
traps: Prorupted states have a panhandle giving access to resources or sea; Perforated states completely surround another (South Africa surrounds Lesotho).

title: Centripetal and Centrifugal Forces
objectives: National identity as centripetal
Devolution as centrifugal
Balkanization

sections.title: Centripetal and Centrifugal Forces
traps: Centripetal forces unite (common language, national anthem); centrifugal forces divide (ethnic conflict, regional autonomy demands) — always give a specific example.

title: Supranationalism and International Organizations
objectives: EU integration and challenges
UN peacekeeping
Trade blocs and sovereignty

sections.title: Supranationalism and International Organizations
traps: Supranationalism = states giving up some sovereignty to a larger body; Brexit is the prime example of a state reasserting sovereignty over supranational membership.

title: Electoral Geography
objectives: Gerrymandering
Reapportionment vs. redistricting
Voting patterns and geography

sections.title: Electoral Geography
traps: Gerrymandering involves 'cracking' (split opponent voters) or 'packing' (concentrate opponent voters) — FRQs show district maps and ask you to identify the technique.

title: Origins and Spread of Agriculture
objectives: First Agricultural Revolution
Hearths (Fertile Crescent, SE Asia)
Domestication of plants and animals

sections.title: Origins and Spread of Agriculture
traps: First Ag Revolution = domestication (~10,000 BCE); Second = mechanization (18th c. Britain); Third = Green Revolution (20th c.) — know all three and their geographic hearths.

title: Von Thünen's Model
objectives: Concentric rings of land use
Distance from market and intensity
Modern critiques

sections.title: Von Thünen's Model
traps: Von Thünen: intensive farming closest to market (dairy, vegetables), extensive farming farther out (grain, ranching) — the model assumes flat plain and single market.

title: Types of Agriculture
objectives: Subsistence vs. commercial
Intensive vs. extensive
Plantation and mixed crop-livestock

sections.title: Types of Agriculture
traps: Shifting cultivation (slash and burn) is subsistence and extensive; market gardening is commercial and intensive — map these terms to Von Thünen rings.

title: Green Revolution and Biotechnology
objectives: High-yield variety seeds
GMOs and food security
Environmental critiques

sections.title: Green Revolution and Biotechnology
traps: Green Revolution increased yields but also increased reliance on fertilizers and water — FRQs ask you to weigh benefits (less hunger) vs. costs (soil degradation, debt).

title: Agriculture and the Environment
objectives: Soil degradation and desertification
Water usage in irrigation
Sustainable agriculture

sections.title: Agriculture and the Environment
traps: The Aral Sea shrinkage is the canonical example of unsustainable irrigation — rivers diverted for cotton farming caused an environmental catastrophe.

title: Origins and Growth of Cities
objectives: Site vs. situation
Central place theory (Christaller)
Urban hierarchy

sections.title: Origins and Growth of Cities
traps: Central place theory: threshold (minimum population to support a service) vs. range (maximum distance customers travel) — larger threshold = higher order place.

title: Urban Land-Use Models
objectives: Concentric Zone (Burgess)
Sector (Hoyt)
Multiple Nuclei (Harris & Ullman)

sections.title: Urban Land-Use Models
traps: Concentric Zone = rings from CBD; Sector = pie slices along transportation; Multiple Nuclei = several nodes — FRQs give a city diagram and ask you to identify the model.

title: Latin American, SE Asian, and Sub-Saharan City Models
objectives: Griffin-Ford Latin American model
McGee model (SE Asia)
Sub-Saharan African city structure

sections.title: Latin American, SE Asian, and Sub-Saharan City Models
traps: Griffin-Ford: spine of commercial activity radiating from CBD with elite housing along it, shanty towns (disamenity zones) at periphery — inverse of US model.

title: Suburbanization and Sprawl
objectives: Edge cities
Boomburbs
Urban sprawl consequences

sections.title: Suburbanization and Sprawl
traps: Edge cities (Tyson's Corner, VA) have more jobs than bedrooms — distinguish from bedroom communities (commuter suburbs with no job centers).

title: Challenges of Urban Growth
objectives: Informal settlements/squatter cities
Urban heat island
Environmental justice

sections.title: Challenges of Urban Growth
traps: Squatter settlements (favelas, bustees, bidonvilles) lack legal title and formal services — know regional terms; FRQs ask you to propose a realistic improvement strategy.

title: Urban Renewal and Gentrification
objectives: Redlining and disinvestment
Gentrification displacement
Smart growth and new urbanism

sections.title: Urban Renewal and Gentrification
traps: Gentrification raises property values, displacing lower-income residents — FRQs ask you to identify winners and losers; New Urbanism advocates walkable, mixed-use design.

title: Economic Development Models
objectives: Rostow's stages of growth
Wallerstein's world-systems theory
Core-periphery model

sections.title: Economic Development Models
traps: Rostow (optimistic ladder): traditional → take-off → drive to maturity; Wallerstein (critical): core exploits periphery — FRQs ask you to critique both models.

title: Development Indicators
objectives: GNI per capita, HDI, GII
GDP vs. GNI distinction
Limitations of single indicators

sections.title: Development Indicators
traps: HDI combines income, education, and life expectancy — higher than GDP rank means good social programs (Cuba); lower means wealth without social investment (Gulf states).

title: Industrial Location Theory
objectives: Weber's least-cost theory
Agglomeration and deglomeration
Footloose industries

sections.title: Industrial Location Theory
traps: Weber: locate at minimum transport cost for inputs + outputs; bulk-gaining industries locate near market; bulk-reducing industries locate near raw materials.

title: Globalization and Trade
objectives: New international division of labor
Commodity chains
Special economic zones

sections.title: Globalization and Trade
traps: Maquiladoras (Mexico–US border) are the canonical SEZ example — cheap labor, lax regulation, export-oriented; commodity chains trace production from raw material to consumer.

title: Sustainable Development
objectives: Brundtland definition
Alternative energy and green technology
Microfinance and NGOs

sections.title: Sustainable Development
traps: Brundtland: 'meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet their own' — quote this definition exactly; FRQs love asking about it.

title: Limits Review and L'Hôpital's Rule — BC Depth
objectives: Converting all to 0/0 or ∞/∞ before applying L'Hôpital's
Limits involving e^x and ln x at infinity

sections.title: Key concepts
traps: Applying L'Hôpital's to 0·∞ directly — must rewrite as 0/0 or ∞/∞ first; AP BC tests the conversion step explicitly

title: Continuity on Closed Intervals and IVT Applications
objectives: IVT to prove existence of solutions
Uniform continuity concept
Lipschitz conditions for uniqueness of ODE solutions

sections.title: Continuity on Closed Intervals and IVT Applications
traps: Not citing both IVT hypotheses (continuity + closed interval) when proving root existence — AP FRQ requires explicit justification, not just 'by IVT'

title: Differentiation Rules — BC Speed and Fluency
objectives: Chain, product, quotient rules in rapid succession
Derivatives of all six trig and inverse trig functions
Implicit differentiation for complex relations

sections.title: Differentiation Rules — BC Speed and Fluency
traps: Slow chain rule execution on multi-layer compositions — BC exam is time-pressured; must recognize and differentiate sin²(e^(x²)) in one pass without step-by-step rewriting

title: Parametric Differentiation and Higher Derivatives
objectives: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt); d²y/dx² = [d/dt(dy/dx)]/(dx/dt)
Concavity of parametric curves from second derivative sign

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: ∫√(x'² + y'²) dt

traps: Computing d²y/dx² as (y'')/(x'') — wrong; must differentiate dy/dx with respect to t, then divide by dx/dt

title: Implicit Differentiation for BC-Level Curves
objectives: Differentiating complex implicit relations with product and chain rules
Finding d²y/dx² implicitly by differentiating dy/dx again
Tangent lines at multiple points on the same curve

sections.title: Implicit Differentiation for BC-Level Curves
traps: Not substituting dy/dx expression when computing second implicit derivative — AP BC gives y²= x³-x and asks for d²y/dx²; must substitute the first derivative result into the second derivative expression

title: Derivatives in Polar Form
objectives: Rate of change of r with respect to θ

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: (dr/dθ · sinθ + r·cosθ)/(dr/dθ · cosθ - r·sinθ)
dy/dθ = 0; vertical tangents: dx/dθ = 0

traps: Finding horizontal tangent by setting dr/dθ = 0 instead of dy/dθ = 0 — horizontal tangent requires y'(θ) = 0 in polar form, not dr/dθ = 0 (that's only tangent to r itself)

title: L'Hôpital's Rule in Applied Contexts
objectives: Indeterminate forms in limits from physical models
Applying L'Hôpital's multiple times when needed
Connection to Taylor series as alternative to L'Hôpital

sections.title: L'Hôpital's Rule in Applied Contexts
traps: Not recognizing when Taylor series is faster than L'Hôpital — for lim (sinx - x)/x³, Taylor expansion is far cleaner; AP BC often rewards either approach but Taylor is less error-prone

title: Optimization and Related Rates — BC Complexity
objectives: Multi-constraint optimization requiring Lagrange multipliers concept
Related rates with implicit geometric relations
Newton's method and iterative root-finding

sections.title: Optimization and Related Rates — BC Complexity
traps: Not verifying which critical point is the global optimum in multi-variable setups — AP BC gives scenarios with multiple critical points; must test all and compare values

title: Graphical Analysis — f, f', f'' Across BC Contexts
objectives: Reading and constructing graphs of f from graphs of f'
Inflection points from sign changes of f''
MVT and Rolle's theorem application in proofs

sections.title: Graphical Analysis — f, f', f'' Across BC Contexts
traps: Identifying local max/min from f' without confirming sign change — AP BC gives graphs of f' with zero crossings; must confirm the sign changes, not just identify zeros

title: Extreme Values in Parametric and Polar Forms
objectives: Finding extrema of r(θ) in polar form
Finding extrema of arc length or area in parametric
Second derivative test for parametric curves

sections.title: Extreme Values in Parametric and Polar Forms
traps: Finding critical θ values from r'(θ) = 0 when looking for max/min of the curve's position — AP BC may ask for the maximum distance from origin, which requires r'(θ)=0, not dy/dθ=0

title: Integration by Parts — When and How
objectives: ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du; LIATE for choosing u
Tabular integration for repeated integration by parts
Definite integrals using integration by parts with limits

sections.title: Integration by Parts — When and How
traps: Choosing u as the function that gets more complicated when differentiated — LIATE: Logarithm, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential; the first applicable type is u

title: Partial Fractions and Rational Integration
objectives: Decomposing A/(x-r)(x-s) into partial fractions
Integrating 1/(x-a) = ln|x-a| + C from partial fractions
Long division first when degree of numerator ≥ denominator

sections.title: Partial Fractions and Rational Integration
traps: Skipping long division when numerator degree ≥ denominator degree — partial fraction decomposition only works for proper fractions; must divide first to get proper rational + polynomial

title: Improper Integrals — Infinite Limits and Discontinuities
objectives: Master Improper Integrals — Infinite Limits and Discontinuities for the Integration and Accumulation of Change unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: infinite limits → ∫ₐ^∞ f dx = lim_{b→∞} ∫ₐᵇ f dx
discontinuous integrand → limit at point of discontinuity
p-integral ∫₁^∞ 1/xᵖ dx converges iff p>1

traps: Evaluating improper integrals without converting to a limit — must write lim and take it explicitly; AP FRQ requires showing the limit notation, not just plugging in ∞

title: u-Substitution and Trig Substitution
objectives: Trig substitution for √(a²-x²), √(a²+x²), √(x²-a²)
Completing the square to prepare for trig substitution or arctan form
Choosing the right substitution from the form of the integrand

sections.title: u-Substitution and Trig Substitution
traps: Using trig substitution without restricting the range of the substitution variable — for x = asinθ, need θ ∈ [-π/2, π/2]; AP BC expects you to show the restriction and convert back correctly

title: Integration of Parametric and Polar Functions
objectives: Master Integration of Parametric and Polar Functions for the Integration and Accumulation of Change unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: A = ∫y dx = ∫y(t)x'(t)dt
A = ½∫r² dθ
L = ∫√(r² + (dr/dθ)²) dθ

traps: Forgetting the factor of ½ in polar area formula — A = ½∫r² dθ (not ∫r² dθ); AP consistently tests this factor; also must correctly identify limits θ₁ and θ₂ from the curve description

title: Separable DEs and Logistic Growth — BC Depth
objectives: Solving logistic DE by partial fractions and integration
Equilibrium stability analysis from sign of dP/dt
Approximating logistic behavior at early (exponential) and late (plateau) stages

sections.title: Separable DEs and Logistic Growth — BC Depth
traps: Not solving the logistic DE fully — AP BC FRQ asks for the explicit solution P(t); must use partial fractions to integrate 1/[P(M-P)] and solve for P

title: Euler's Method and Numerical Error Analysis
objectives: Comparing Euler's method accuracy at different step sizes
Error direction from concavity of solution curve
Improved Euler (Heun's) method concept

sections.title: Euler's Method and Numerical Error Analysis
traps: Not connecting Euler error direction to concavity — Euler overestimates when concave down, underestimates when concave up; AP BC asks to justify whether the approximation is an over or underestimate

title: Area and Volume — BC Integration Methods
objectives: Volume from parametric curves
Shell, disk, washer for all rotation axes

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: A = ½∫(r_outer² - r_inner²)dθ

traps: Using incorrect limits for area between polar curves — find intersections by setting r₁(θ)=r₂(θ); the limits must correctly capture the region; AP BC gives two polar curves and expects the correct setup

title: Arc Length in Multiple Coordinate Systems
objectives: Master Arc Length in Multiple Coordinate Systems for the Applications of Integration unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: L = ∫√(x'²+y'²)dt
L = ∫√(r²+(dr/dθ)²)dθ

traps: Mixing up which arc length formula applies — AP BC gives a curve in one of three forms; must identify the form and apply the corresponding formula; polar arc length is the most commonly confused

unitName: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates, and Vector-Valued Functions
title: Parametric Equations — Full Analysis
objectives: Eliminating parameter to find Cartesian form
dy/dx and d²y/dx² for parametric curves
Speed = √(x'² + y'²); distance traveled = ∫speed dt

sections.title: Parametric Equations — Full Analysis
traps: Computing distance as displacement (∫velocity components separately) — total distance traveled requires integrating speed = √(x'²+y'²), not integrating x'(t) and y'(t) separately

unitName: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates, and Vector-Valued Functions
title: Polar Coordinates — Conversion and Graphing
objectives: Converting between polar (r,θ) and Cartesian (x,y)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: rose curves, limaçons, cardioids, spirals
replacing θ with -θ, π-θ

traps: Not identifying the type of polar curve before graphing — AP BC gives r = 2+3cosθ (limaçon with inner loop) and expects you to sketch it; recognizing curve type from the equation form is essential

unitName: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates, and Vector-Valued Functions
title: Area and Arc Length in Polar
objectives: Area between polar curves using outer minus inner
Finding intersection points of polar curves (including pole)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: area swept by radius vector

traps: Missing intersections at the pole — two curves can both pass through the origin at DIFFERENT θ values; AP BC tests whether you find ALL intersections, including the pole as a special case

unitName: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates, and Vector-Valued Functions
title: Vector-Valued Functions — Calculus
objectives: r(t) = x(t)î + y(t)ĵ; r'(t) = velocity vector
Speed, displacement, total distance from vector functions
Unit tangent vector T = r'/|r'|

sections.title: Vector-Valued Functions — Calculus
traps: Confusing velocity vector with speed — velocity is r'(t) (a vector with direction); speed is |r'(t)| (a scalar); AP BC tests that displacement uses ∫r'(t)dt while total distance uses ∫|r'(t)|dt

unitName: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates, and Vector-Valued Functions
title: Vector-Valued Functions — Motion in 2D
objectives: Position from velocity by integration with initial condition
Acceleration vector and its decomposition into tangential and normal components
Curvature κ = |r' × r''|/|r'|³

sections.title: Vector-Valued Functions — Motion in 2D
traps: Not using vector integration correctly — ∫r'(t)dt + r(0) gives position; must integrate EACH component and add the initial position vector component-by-component

title: Convergence of Sequences
objectives: L'Hôpital for sequence limits involving ∞/∞ or 0/0
Squeeze theorem for sequences

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: bounded + monotone → converges

traps: Confusing sequence convergence with series convergence — a sequence {aₙ} can converge even if the series Σaₙ diverges (e.g., aₙ = 1/n converges to 0 but Σ1/n diverges); AP BC tests this distinction

title: Series Convergence Tests — The Full Toolkit
objectives: Comparison, limit comparison, ratio, root, integral tests

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Σarⁿ converges iff |r|<1, sum = a/(1-r)
Σ1/nᵖ converges iff p>1

traps: Using the ratio test for p-series or geometric series — ratio test gives inconclusive result (L=1) for p-series; use p-series test directly; AP BC tests choosing the right convergence test for the given series

title: Alternating Series and Error Bound
objectives: Absolute vs. conditional convergence distinction

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: alternating signs, decreasing |aₙ|→0
|error| ≤ first omitted term

traps: Thinking alternating series always converge — must verify terms are decreasing AND approach 0; if |aₙ| doesn't approach 0, even an alternating series diverges; AP tests this necessary condition

title: Power Series — Radius and Interval of Convergence
objectives: Ratio test to find radius of convergence R
Testing endpoints separately (ratio test gives inconclusive at endpoints)
Interval of convergence vs. radius of convergence

sections.title: Power Series — Radius and Interval of Convergence
traps: Forgetting to test endpoints after finding the radius — the interval of convergence requires checking both endpoints by substitution; each may converge or diverge and must be tested separately

title: Taylor and Maclaurin Series — Building Polynomial Approximations
objectives: Building new series from known ones by substitution and differentiation

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Σ[f^(n)(a)/n!](x-a)ⁿ
eˣ, sinx, cosx, 1/(1-x), ln(1+x)

traps: Not using known Maclaurin series to build new ones — AP BC gives sin(x²) and expects substitution into the sinx series, not re-deriving; building from known series is faster and less error-prone

title: Taylor Polynomial Error — Lagrange Remainder
objectives: Using error bound to determine degree needed for given accuracy
Comparing Taylor error to alternating series error bound

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: |error| ≤ M|x-a|^(n+1)/(n+1)! where M = max|f^(n+1)|

traps: Finding M as the derivative value at c instead of the maximum value on the interval — M must be the MAXIMUM of |f^(n+1)| on the entire interval from a to x; AP asks for the error bound, requiring correct M identification

title: Operations on Power Series
objectives: Differentiating and integrating power series term-by-term (valid within ROC)
Multiplying power series for products like eˣsinx
Using ∫power series to compute ∫(sinx/x)dx type integrals

sections.title: Operations on Power Series
traps: Differentiating/integrating power series and forgetting to adjust the constant C and the shifted index — AP BC asks to use the series for 1/(1-x) to find a series for ln(1-x) by integrating; must include +C

title: Series in Applied Problems — Using Taylor Polynomials
objectives: Approximating function values with degree-n Taylor polynomial
Using series to evaluate difficult limits (better than L'Hôpital for some)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: when is a Taylor approximation 'good enough'?

traps: Not using Taylor series to simplify limit problems — lim(1-cosx)/x² is easy with Taylor (cosx ≈ 1 - x²/2 + ...) but tedious with L'Hôpital applied twice; AP BC rewards recognizing the more efficient approach

title: Classifying Variables and Study Design
objectives: Categorical vs. quantitative; discrete vs. continuous
Voluntary response bias and why such samples are unreliable

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: why experiments can show causation

traps: Confusing association with causation from observational data — correlation from an observational study cannot establish causation; AP FRQ expects 'association' not 'cause' language for non-experimental data

title: Displaying Data — Graphs and Their Interpretation
objectives: Comparing two distributions on the same scale

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: when each is appropriate
SOCS (shape, outliers, center, spread)

traps: Describing histograms without all four SOCS components — AP FRQ always requires shape, center, spread, AND outliers; missing any component loses partial credit

title: Measures of Center — Mean vs. Median
objectives: When to prefer each measure of center in context

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: sensitive to outliers; median: resistant to outliers
mean pulled toward tail, median stays near center

traps: Using mean to describe a skewed distribution — for skewed income data, the median is more representative; AP asks to choose AND justify which measure is more appropriate given the shape

title: Measures of Spread — Standard Deviation and IQR
objectives: 1.5×IQR rule for identifying outliers

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: resistant to outliers; used with median
sensitive to outliers; used with mean

traps: Applying the standard deviation outlier rule instead of 1.5×IQR — for box plots and five-number summaries, the 1.5×IQR rule applies; standard deviation-based rules are for normal distributions; AP tests which is appropriate

title: Normal Distribution and the Empirical Rule
objectives: 68-95-99.7 rule for normal distributions
Using z-table to find proportions and percentiles

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: z = (x-μ)/σ; z-score interpretation

traps: Applying the empirical rule without confirming normality — the 68-95-99.7 rule ONLY applies to normal distributions; AP gives a distribution and may not confirm normality; must check before applying

title: z-Scores, Percentiles, and Normal Probability
objectives: Converting between x-values and z-scores
Finding probability P(a < X < b) from z-table

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: finding x given a percentile

traps: Using the z-score formula with sample mean (x̄) instead of population mean (μ) when finding individual observation probabilities — z = (x-μ)/σ for individual values; z = (x̄-μ)/(σ/√n) for sample means

title: Boxplots and Five-Number Summary
objectives: Minimum, Q1, Median, Q3, Maximum and how to compute each
Comparing distributions using side-by-side boxplots

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: outliers displayed as individual points

traps: Plotting suspected outliers in the box or whisker instead of as separate dots — AP specifically requires identifying and plotting outliers (beyond 1.5×IQR from quartiles) as individual points in modified boxplots

title: Density Curves and the Area-as-Probability Convention
objectives: Normal density curve properties and connection to probability

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: area under curve = probability; total area = 1
flat density curve, equal areas for equal intervals

traps: Treating the height of a density curve as probability — height is density (probability per unit interval), not probability; only AREA gives probability; AP tests this with uniform distributions where height > 1 is possible

title: Scatterplots and Correlation
objectives: Correlation does not imply causation — lurking variables

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: direction, form, strength, outliers
measures linear association only, ranges from -1 to +1

traps: Using r to describe non-linear associations — r only measures linear strength; a strong curved relationship can have r ≈ 0; AP gives a curved scatterplot and tests whether r is an appropriate summary

title: Least-Squares Regression Line — Interpretation
objectives: ŷ = a + bx; slope b = r(sy/sx); intercept a = ȳ - bx̄
Interpreting intercept in context (often not meaningful)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: predicted change in y per unit increase in x

traps: Describing slope without 'predicted' — in regression, the slope gives the PREDICTED (or average) change; for one specific observation the change may differ; AP FRQ deducts for missing 'predicted' or 'average'

title: Residuals and Assessing Linearity
objectives: Residual = observed - predicted = y - ŷ
Patterns in residual plot (curves, fans) indicate model problems

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: random scatter indicates good linear fit

traps: Calling a residual plot 'random' without looking for patterns — a curve in residuals means linear model is wrong; a funnel means non-constant variance; AP gives a residual plot and asks to interpret adequacy of the model

title: R² — Coefficient of Determination
objectives: R² = proportion of variation in y explained by linear relationship with x
R² ranges from 0 to 1; larger = better fit

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: R² = r² for simple linear regression

traps: Interpreting r² as 'r squared percent' — must say 'r² of the variation in y is explained by the linear relationship with x'; AP FRQ requires the full contextual interpretation with units/variables named

title: Influential Points and Leverage
objectives: Master Influential Points and Leverage for the Exploring Two-Variable Data unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: large |residual|, poor fit to line
extreme x value, may not have large residual
removal substantially changes the regression line

traps: Confusing outlier (large residual) with influential point (changes the line when removed) — a high-leverage point on the regression line has small residual but is still influential; AP tests these as distinct concepts

title: Transformations to Achieve Linearity
objectives: Log or square root transformation to linearize curved data
Identifying which transformation achieves linearity from residual plots

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: log(y) vs. log(x); exponential model: log(y) vs. x

traps: Applying a transformation without verifying it achieves linearity — AP gives a residual plot after transformation and expects confirmation that the pattern is now random; linearization must be verified, not assumed

title: Two-Way Tables and Association in Categorical Data
objectives: Marginal, joint, and conditional distributions from two-way tables

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: conditional distributions differ across categories
direction of association reverses when data is combined

traps: Using marginal frequencies instead of conditional frequencies to assess association — must compare conditional distributions (row or column percentages); AP gives a two-way table and asks whether variables are associated

title: Causation, Correlation, and Confounding
objectives: Why randomized experiments can establish causation but observational studies can't

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: causation, common cause, coincidence
associated with both X and Y

traps: Describing a confounding variable as one that 'affects the outcome' — it must also be associated with the explanatory variable; AP FRQ asks to 'identify and explain' a potential confounding variable, requiring both parts

title: Sampling Methods — Which to Use and Why
objectives: Master Sampling Methods — Which to Use and Why for the Collecting Data unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: every individual equally likely to be chosen
divide into strata, SRS within each
divide into groups, randomly select entire groups; systematic sampling

traps: Confusing stratified with cluster sampling — stratified takes a few from EACH group; cluster sampling takes ALL from SOME groups; AP gives a sampling description and asks to identify the method

title: Sampling Bias and Its Sources
objectives: Wording effects in survey questions

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: mechanisms of each
self-selected samples overrepresent extreme opinions

traps: Calling any sampling error 'bias' — bias is SYSTEMATIC error in one direction; random sampling error is expected and decreases with sample size; AP tests whether a described error is bias or random variation

title: Experimental Design — The Three Principles
objectives: Control group vs. placebo group (not the same)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: why each is necessary
single-blind and double-blind designs

traps: Confusing control group with placebo group — control group receives no treatment; placebo group receives an inert treatment; both are controls, but AP distinguishes why placebos are used (to account for psychological effects)

title: Blocking in Experiments
objectives: Why blocking reduces variability and increases sensitivity to treatment effects

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: grouping similar experimental units before randomization
simplest block design (pairing individuals or before/after)

traps: Describing blocking as 'randomly dividing into groups' — blocking is NOT random; you group similar units first, then randomize within blocks; AP asks to identify what constitutes an appropriate blocking variable

title: Causation in Experiments
objectives: Random assignment allows causal conclusions (unlike random sampling)
Four conditions for establishing causation

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: random sample allows generalization; random assignment allows causation

traps: Claiming random sampling establishes causation — random SAMPLING allows generalization to the population; random ASSIGNMENT allows causal conclusions; AP tests this two-condition distinction for scope of inference

title: Ethics in Data Collection
objectives: Informed consent, anonymity vs. confidentiality, IRB oversight
Ethical issues in observational vs. experimental research
Data privacy and protection

sections.title: Ethics in Data Collection
traps: Confusing anonymity (researcher doesn't know identity) with confidentiality (researcher knows but won't disclose) — AP occasionally tests these distinctions and why they matter for bias and participant protection

title: Simulation in Statistics
objectives: Designing a simulation to model a probability problem
Assigning digits/outcomes to represent probabilities
Running repetitions and computing empirical probability from results

sections.title: Simulation in Statistics
traps: Assigning multiple digits to the same outcome without justifying the proportion — if P(success) = 0.3, must assign exactly 30 of 100 equally-likely outcomes; AP FRQ asks to describe simulation design clearly and precisely

title: Survey Design and Question Wording
objectives: Loaded questions, leading questions, and double-barreled questions
Order effects in survey items
Pilot testing and question validation

sections.title: Survey Design and Question Wording
traps: Not identifying the specific type of bias in a survey question — AP asks to identify AND explain the source; saying 'it's biased' without naming the mechanism (e.g., response bias from question wording) loses points

unitName: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
title: Probability Rules — Addition and Multiplication
objectives: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B); simplifies if mutually exclusive
P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B|A); simplifies if independent

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: P(Aᶜ) = 1 - P(A)

traps: Applying the simplified multiplication rule P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B) without checking independence — must first verify independence; AP gives probabilities and tests whether events are independent before using the product rule

unitName: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
title: Conditional Probability and Independence
objectives: Testing independence from a two-way table

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: conditional probability formula
P(A|B) = P(A); knowing B doesn't change probability of A

traps: Confusing mutually exclusive with independent — mutually exclusive events (P(A and B)=0) are NOT independent (unless P(A)=0); if two events can't occur together, knowing one occurred tells you something about the other

unitName: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
title: Discrete Random Variables — Expected Value and Variance
objectives: Var(X) = Σ[(x-μ)²·P(X=x)]; SD(X) = √Var(X)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: probability-weighted average
E(aX+b) = aE(X)+b; Var(aX+b) = a²Var(X)

traps: Adding standard deviations instead of variances — Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) for independent X, Y; SD(X+Y) ≠ SD(X) + SD(Y); must add variances first, then take square root

unitName: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
title: Binomial Distribution
objectives: P(X=k) = C(n,k)pᵏ(1-p)^(n-k)
μ = np; σ = √(np(1-p)); normal approximation when np≥10 and n(1-p)≥10

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: BINS (Binary, Independent, fixed N, same p)

traps: Using binomial when independence assumption is violated — sampling without replacement from small populations violates independence; must check whether n is less than 10% of population for independence to hold approximately

unitName: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
title: Geometric Distribution
objectives: E(X) = 1/p; Var(X) = (1-p)/p²

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: number of trials until first success
geometric has no fixed n

traps: Confusing binomial (count of successes in fixed n trials) with geometric (number of trials until first success) — AP gives a scenario and tests which distribution applies; the presence or absence of a fixed number of trials is the key distinction

unitName: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
title: Continuous Probability Distributions
objectives: P(X=a) = 0 for continuous distributions; only intervals have nonzero probability

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: f(x) = 1/(b-a) on [a,b]
F(x) = P(X≤x) = cumulative area

traps: Computing P(X=2.5) as nonzero for a continuous distribution — for continuous distributions, single values have probability zero; must compute P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = area; AP gives an interval and expects area calculation

unitName: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
title: Normal Distribution Calculations
objectives: Standardizing to Z and using z-table or calculator normalcdf
Finding values from percentiles using invNorm

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: X+Y still normal if X, Y normal

traps: Not recognizing that a sum of normal random variables is also normal — AP gives the means and variances of two normal RVs and asks for probabilities about their sum; must compute new mean = μ₁+μ₂ and variance = σ₁²+σ₂² first

unitName: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
title: Law of Large Numbers and Simulation
objectives: Using simulation to estimate probabilities empirically

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: sample proportion approaches true probability as n grows
past outcomes don't change future probabilities in independent trials

traps: Confusing LLN (proportion converges) with the gambler's fallacy (each trial has changed probability to 'balance out') — individual trials are independent; LLN is about long-run averages, not any specific next outcome

title: Sampling Distribution of p̂
objectives: p̂ is the sample proportion; its sampling distribution is approximately normal for large n

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: μ_p̂ = p; spread: σ_p̂ = √(p(1-p)/n)
np ≥ 10 and n(1-p) ≥ 10 for normality

traps: Using the formula σ_p̂ = √(p̂(1-p̂)/n) with the observed p̂ instead of the true p — when the true p is known (null hypothesis), use p; only substitute p̂ when p is unknown (confidence intervals)

title: Sampling Distribution of x̄
objectives: μ_x̄ = μ; σ_x̄ = σ/√n (standard error)
Population must be normal OR n large for x̄ to be normal

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: x̄ is approximately normal for n ≥ 30 regardless of population shape

traps: Applying CLT to small samples from skewed populations — CLT requires n ≥ 30 (approximately) for non-normal populations; if n=10 and population is skewed, x̄ is NOT approximately normal

title: Central Limit Theorem — The Key Insight
objectives: CLT applies to means, not individual observations
Population distribution vs. sampling distribution of x̄

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: averaging many random values concentrates the distribution

traps: Applying CLT to individual observations — CLT describes the distribution of SAMPLE MEANS, not individual data values; P(X > 5) for one randomly chosen value uses the original distribution, not the normal approximation

title: Sampling Distributions for Differences
objectives: Independence assumption required between samples

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: center = p₁-p₂; variance = p₁(1-p₁)/n₁ + p₂(1-p₂)/n₂
center = μ₁-μ₂; variance = σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂

traps: Adding standard errors instead of variances when combining two sampling distributions — must add VARIANCES and then take the square root; SE(x̄₁ - x̄₂) = √(σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂)

title: Bias and Variability of Estimators
objectives: Bias-variance tradeoff in statistical estimation

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: E(estimator) = parameter
smaller standard error = more precise estimator

traps: Confusing bias (systematic error) with variability (precision) — an estimator can be unbiased but imprecise (high variance) or precise but biased; AP asks to describe an estimator in terms of BOTH properties

title: Effect of Sample Size on Sampling Distributions
objectives: Doubling n reduces SE by factor of √2, not 2
Sampling distribution narrowing as n increases visualized

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: smaller standard error (SE = σ/√n)

traps: Saying 'larger sample gives smaller standard deviation' — larger sample reduces the STANDARD ERROR (of the mean), not the population standard deviation or individual observation variability; AP tests this language precision

title: t-Distribution vs. z-Distribution
objectives: t-distribution approaches z as degrees of freedom → ∞

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: heavier tails, used when σ unknown; degrees of freedom = n-1
t* > z* for same confidence level (heavier tails require wider interval)

traps: Using z* instead of t* when σ is unknown — whenever population standard deviation is unknown (almost always in practice), must use t*; AP tests when each distribution is appropriate

title: Conditions for Inference — The Three Checks
objectives: Master Conditions for Inference — The Three Checks for the Sampling Distributions unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: data from random sample or randomized experiment
n≥30 or normal population or no strong skew
population ≥ 10n (10% condition)

traps: Skipping condition checks and going straight to calculations — AP FRQ requires explicitly stating, checking, and verifying all three conditions; missing any condition check typically costs 1 point on the scoring rubric

title: Confidence Intervals for One Proportion
objectives: CI: p̂ ± z*(√(p̂(1-p̂)/n)); using p̂ (not p) in SE for CI
Margin of error, confidence level, sample size relationships

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: 'We are 95% confident the true proportion is in...'

traps: Saying 'there is a 95% probability the true proportion is in this interval' — the true proportion is FIXED (not random); the interval either contains it or not; correct language is 'we are 95% confident'

title: Significance Tests for One Proportion
objectives: H₀: p = p₀ vs. Hₐ: p ≠ p₀ (two-sided) or one-sided

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: z = (p̂ - p₀)/√(p₀(1-p₀)/n); using p₀ in SE for tests
probability of getting this result or more extreme IF H₀ true

traps: Using p̂ in the standard error for hypothesis tests — for hypothesis tests, use p₀ (null hypothesis value) in the SE formula; p̂ is used only for confidence intervals; this distinction appears on almost every AP stats FRQ

title: Two-Sample Proportion Tests and Intervals
objectives: Large sample conditions for each sample must be checked separately

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: use pooled proportion p_c in SE
use separate p̂₁ and p̂₂ in SE (no pooling)

traps: Using pooled proportion for confidence intervals — pooling only happens in hypothesis tests when H₀: p₁=p₂; for CIs (no assumption of equal proportions), use unpooled standard error with p̂₁ and p̂₂ separately

title: Type I and Type II Errors and Power
objectives: Power = 1 - β; increases with larger n, larger effect size, larger α

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: rejecting true H₀; probability = α (significance level)
failing to reject false H₀; probability = β

traps: Confusing Type I and II error in context — AP gives a specific scenario and asks which type of error is described; Type I = falsely concluding there's an effect; Type II = missing a real effect

title: P-value Interpretation — The Most Tested Concept
objectives: Small p-value = evidence against H₀; NOT probability H₀ is true
Significance level α as the threshold for rejection

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: probability of observed statistic OR MORE EXTREME, given H₀ is true

traps: Saying 'the p-value is the probability H₀ is true' — this is false; p-value is P(data at least this extreme | H₀ is true); AP FRQ requires the conditional statement structure in the interpretation

title: Confidence Interval as a Range of Plausible Values
objectives: CI informs us about plausible parameter values, not just significance

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.term: Confidence level as long-run capture rate
terms.def: 95% of CIs contain the true value

terms.term: Connection between CI and two-sided test
terms.def: parameter outside CI ↔ reject H₀

traps: Interpreting confidence level as probability for ONE interval — once an interval is computed, the true parameter either is or isn't in it; the 95% refers to the METHOD over many samples, not this specific interval

title: Conditions for Proportion Inference
objectives: Master Conditions for Proportion Inference for the Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions unit.
