sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: random sample
np₀ ≥ 10 and n(1-p₀) ≥ 10 (using p₀ for tests)
n ≤ 10% of population

traps: Using p̂ instead of p₀ in the normal condition check for hypothesis tests — must use the NULL hypothesis value p₀ when checking np₀ ≥ 10; this differs from the CI check which uses p̂

title: Selecting the Right Test — One vs. Two Sample
objectives: Master Selecting the Right Test — One vs. Two Sample for the Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: comparing one group to a known standard
comparing two independent groups
two measurements on same subject → one-sample on differences

traps: Using two-sample test for matched pairs data — matched pairs are NOT independent samples; must compute differences first, then apply one-sample t-test to the differences; AP gives the design and tests whether you identify it correctly

title: One-Sample t-Test and t-Interval
objectives: Using t-table or calculator; df = n-1 for one sample

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: test statistic with degrees of freedom n-1

traps: Using z-procedures when σ is unknown — whenever you use s (sample standard deviation) instead of σ, use t-procedures; almost all real-world problems require t

title: Two-Sample t-Procedures
objectives: Checking conditions separately for each sample

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: df calculated by calculator (Welch) or conservative df = min(n₁,n₂)-1
(x̄₁ - x̄₂) ± t*(SE)

traps: Using the pooled t-test instead of Welch's for two-sample tests — AP Statistics uses Welch's two-sample t (not pooled) by default; pooled is only valid if variances are known to be equal (rarely appropriate)

title: Matched Pairs t-Procedures
objectives: Compute d = x₁ - x₂ for each pair; analyze d as one-sample
t = (d̄ - 0)/(sₐ/√n); df = n-1 (n = number of pairs)
Why matched pairs reduces variability compared to two independent samples

sections.title: Matched Pairs t-Procedures
traps: Treating matched pairs as two independent samples — two measurements on same individual are not independent; must compute differences; AP gives a before-after study and tests whether you use the difference approach

title: Checking Conditions for Means Inference
objectives: Random condition, Normal/Large Sample (n≥30 or normal population), Independence (10% rule)
When to check for outliers for small samples (n<30)
What to do when conditions are not fully met

sections.title: Checking Conditions for Means Inference
traps: Checking conditions only once for the whole test — for two-sample procedures, must check conditions for EACH sample separately; AP FRQ rubrics award partial credit for checking conditions

title: Interpreting Confidence Intervals for Means
objectives: 'We are 95% confident the true mean is between A and B'
Margin of error and how to reduce it
Does CI include null value? Connection to two-sided test

sections.title: Interpreting Confidence Intervals for Means
traps: Interpreting CI as 'probability' — use 'confident' not 'probability' language; the parameter is fixed; AP FRQ consistently tests the exact wording of CI interpretations

title: Statistical Significance vs. Practical Significance
objectives: Large samples can make trivial differences statistically significant

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: p < α; practically significant: meaningful effect size
Cohen's d, confidence interval width

traps: Stopping at 'statistically significant' without addressing practical significance — AP FRQ asks to interpret results in context; a statistically significant difference of 0.01 mm may have no real-world importance

title: Errors in t-Procedures and Robustness
objectives: t-procedures are robust to non-normality when n is large
Nonparametric alternatives when normality fails for small samples

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: heavy skew with small n

traps: Using t-procedures blindly for any quantitative data — if n=5 and the distribution is heavily skewed, the t-distribution approximation is poor; AP asks whether the procedure is appropriate given the distribution and sample size

title: Designing Studies for Specific Inference Goals
objectives: Connecting study design choices to inference conclusions

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: n = (z*σ/ME)² for desired margin of error
sample size needed to detect a given effect

traps: Forgetting to round UP when computing required sample size — n must be a whole number; always round up (e.g., n=64.1 → use n=65); using n=64 gives margin of error slightly larger than desired

title: Chi-Square Goodness of Fit Test
objectives: H₀: specified distribution is correct; χ² = Σ(O-E)²/E
Expected counts from null hypothesis proportions × total n
df = number of categories - 1

sections.title: Chi-Square Goodness of Fit Test
traps: Computing expected counts as equal for each category by default — expected counts come from the NULL HYPOTHESIS proportions, not 1/k; AP gives hypothesized proportions that are not all equal

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence
objectives: H₀: variables are independent; Hₐ: there is an association
Expected count = (row total × column total) / grand total
df = (rows-1)(columns-1)

sections.title: Chi-Square Test of Independence
traps: Confusing chi-square test of independence with chi-square GOF — test of independence uses a two-way table and tests association between TWO categorical variables; GOF tests if ONE variable matches a specified distribution

title: Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity
objectives: Comparing distributions of one categorical variable across multiple groups
Same formula as independence test but different hypotheses and study design
Recognizing when homogeneity vs. independence is appropriate

sections.title: Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity
traps: Using independence test language for a homogeneity study — if data came from separate random samples, it's a test of homogeneity (are distributions the same?); if ONE sample was classified two ways, it's independence

title: Expected Counts and the Chi-Square Distribution
objectives: Expected counts must all be ≥ 5 for chi-square approximation to be valid
Chi-square distribution is right-skewed; always use upper tail for p-value
Relationship between chi-square statistic and degree of departure from H₀

sections.title: Expected Counts and the Chi-Square Distribution
traps: Checking that observed (not expected) counts are ≥ 5 — the condition is on EXPECTED counts (row×column/n), not observed; AP FRQ asks to verify this condition; using observed counts is wrong

title: Post-Hoc Analysis After Chi-Square
objectives: Identifying which cells contribute most to the chi-square statistic
Standardized residuals (O-E)/√E for cell-level analysis
Direction of association not captured by chi-square (only strength)

sections.title: Post-Hoc Analysis After Chi-Square
traps: Reporting only the p-value without identifying where the association is strongest — chi-square tells you IF there's an association; to describe WHERE, examine the largest (O-E)²/E terms; AP FRQ asks to describe what the test reveals

title: Conditions for Regression Inference
objectives: Normal probability plot of residuals

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Linear, Independent errors, Normal errors, Equal variance, Random
random pattern, constant spread, no outliers

traps: Not examining the residual plot before conducting inference — AP FRQ gives a residual plot and asks whether conditions are met; must look for pattern (linearity), funnel shape (equal variance), and normality

title: t-Test for Regression Slope
objectives: H₀: β = 0 (no linear relationship); Hₐ: β ≠ 0
t = b/SE_b with df = n-2

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: probability of getting this slope or steeper by chance if true slope is 0

traps: Confusing the t-statistic for slope with the t for means — for regression slope, df = n-2 (one df lost for each estimated parameter: slope and intercept); AP gives computer output and expects correct df identification

title: Confidence Interval for Regression Slope
objectives: b ± t*(SE_b) gives CI for true slope β
Using computer output to extract b and SE_b

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: plausible values for the rate of change in y per unit x

traps: Interpreting CI for slope without contextual units and variables — AP requires 'We are 95% confident the true slope is between [A] and [B] [y units] per [x unit]'; must use context-specific language

title: Reading Computer Output for Regression
objectives: Identifying coefficients, SE, t-statistic, p-value from printout
Coefficient of determination R² and its interpretation
Using output to construct hypothesis tests and confidence intervals

sections.title: Reading Computer Output for Regression
traps: Not knowing where the slope SE is in computer output — AP gives a standard regression table; the SE for the slope is in the 'Std. Err' column next to the slope coefficient; students often use SE for intercept instead

title: Variables, Data Types, and Literals
objectives: Variable declaration and initialization

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: storage and range
1 vs 1.0 vs true vs 'a'

traps: Assigning a double to an int without casting — int x = 3.7 is a compile error; must cast: int x = (int)3.7 gives 3 (truncates, doesn't round); AP tests this implicit vs explicit casting distinction

title: Operators, Precedence, and Integer Division
objectives: Master Operators, Precedence, and Integer Division for the Primitive Types unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: +, -, *, /, % with type promotion rules
*, /, % before +, -; left-to-right for equal precedence

traps: Not recognizing integer division — 5/2 = 2 in Java, not 2.5; to get 2.5, at least one operand must be a double: 5.0/2 = 2.5; AP tests code with integer division producing unexpected truncated results

title: Type Casting and Type Compatibility
objectives: Casting in mixed-type expressions

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: int → double automatically; narrowing: double → int requires explicit cast

terms.term: Loss of information in narrowing cast

traps: Thinking (int)3.9 rounds to 4 — Java casting truncates toward zero; 3.9 becomes 3 and -3.9 becomes -3; AP gives a cast expression and expects the truncated result

title: Expressions and Assignment
objectives: Assignment returns the assigned value

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: ++i vs i++; prefix vs postfix in expressions

traps: Confusing pre-increment (++i: increment first, use new value) with post-increment (i++: use old value, then increment) — AP gives i++ inside an expression like j = i++ and tests that j gets the original value of i

title: Objects, References, and the null Value
objectives: Objects are accessed via references; two variables can reference the same object
new keyword creating object and calling constructor

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: no object referenced; calling method on null → NullPointerException

traps: Assuming two variables with the same values are the same object — they might not be; .equals() tests value equality; == tests reference equality; AP tests this with String comparisons

title: String Methods and Immutability
objectives: String concatenation with + and the auto-conversion to String

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: methods return new String, don't modify original
length(), substring(a,b), indexOf(), equals(), compareTo()

traps: Assuming s.toUpperCase() modifies s — it doesn't; must do s = s.toUpperCase() to 'update' s (actually creates a new String object); AP gives code that calls a String method without capturing the return value and asks for output

title: Math Class Static Methods
objectives: Math.abs(), Math.pow(), Math.sqrt(), Math.random()
Math.random() returns [0.0, 1.0); generating integers in a range

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: called on the class, not an instance

traps: Off-by-one in Math.random() range calculations — for integers 1 to n: (int)(Math.random() * n) + 1; for 0 to n-1: (int)(Math.random() * n); AP tests code where the range is [min, max] inclusive requiring careful formula

title: Wrapper Classes and Autoboxing
objectives: Integer, Double wrapping primitive types for use in collections

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: automatic conversion between int and Integer
Integer.parseInt(), Integer.MAX_VALUE

traps: Confusing int (primitive) with Integer (object) — Integer can be null; int cannot; autoboxing a null Integer to int throws NullPointerException; AP tests scenarios where null unboxing causes errors

title: Boolean Expressions and Logical Operators
objectives: Comparing with ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: truth tables and short-circuit evaluation

traps: Not applying short-circuit evaluation — in A && B, if A is false, B is never evaluated (and may cause a NullPointerException if evaluated); AP tests code where short-circuit prevents an error

title: if-else if-else Chains
objectives: Dangling else problem

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: only first true condition executes
different behavior when multiple conditions true

traps: Not recognizing that else-if only runs when all previous conditions were false — if the first condition matches, subsequent else-if conditions are never even checked; AP gives a chain and asks for output when multiple conditions could be true

title: String Comparison and == vs. equals()
objectives: == compares references; .equals() compares content for Strings
String literals may be interned (same reference); new String always different reference
equalsIgnoreCase() for case-insensitive comparison

sections.title: String Comparison and == vs. equals()
traps: Using == to compare String content — == tests reference equality; two Strings with the same characters but created separately have different references; AP specifically tests this with new String("hello") == "hello" being false

title: Compound Boolean Conditions and Code Tracing
objectives: Tracing code with complex boolean conditions step by step
Completeness and exclusivity of if-else branches

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: simplification and De Morgan's

traps: Not tracing through compound conditions carefully — AP gives multi-condition if statements with &&, ||, ! and asks for the exact output; must evaluate each sub-expression in order with short-circuit rules

title: while Loops — Trace and Predict
objectives: while condition evaluated before each iteration; loop exits when false
Infinite loop when condition never becomes false
Loop variable update to ensure termination

sections.title: while Loops — Trace and Predict
traps: Forgetting that while condition is checked before EACH iteration, not just before entering — if an update makes the condition false mid-loop, the rest of the loop body still executes; the check happens at the top

title: for Loops — Structure and Equivalence
objectives: Master for Loops — Structure and Equivalence for the Iteration unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: three parts and their execution order
< vs <= in the condition
iteration count = outer count × inner count

traps: Off-by-one in loop bounds — for(int i=0; i<n; i++) executes n times (0 to n-1); for(int i=1; i<=n; i++) also executes n times (1 to n); AP gives array traversal loops where < vs <= determines whether the last element is processed

title: String Traversal with Loops
objectives: Building result strings with concatenation in loop vs. StringBuilder

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: 0 to length()-1
for(int i=0; i<s.length(); i++) and charAt(i)

traps: Using <= s.length() in the loop condition — valid indices are 0 to length()-1; using <= causes a StringIndexOutOfBoundsException on the last iteration; AP tests boundary conditions in string loops

title: Loop Patterns — Accumulator, Search, Count
objectives: Master Loop Patterns — Accumulator, Search, Count for the Iteration unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: sum = 0; sum += element
boolean found = false; set true when found
count++ when condition met

traps: Not initializing accumulator before the loop — if sum is declared inside the loop, it resets to 0 each iteration; AP gives code with initialization in wrong location and asks for the buggy output

title: Nested Loops — Patterns and Output
objectives: Inner loop count depends on outer loop variable

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: triangles, grids, tables
O(n²) for n×n traversal

traps: Mistracing nested loop output — must track BOTH outer and inner loop variables simultaneously; AP gives nested loops and asks for exact printed output; common error is losing track of newlines vs. spaces

title: do-while and break/continue
objectives: Master do-while and break/continue for the Iteration unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: body executes at least once; condition checked at end
exits innermost loop immediately
skips to next iteration of innermost loop

traps: Thinking break exits all nested loops — break only exits the INNERMOST loop it's in; to exit multiple levels of nesting, need a flag variable or labeled break; AP tests this with double-nested loops

title: for-each Loops and Their Limitations
objectives: Cannot use for-each to modify array elements (index needed)
Cannot iterate backward or skip elements with for-each

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: collection): simplified iteration without index

traps: Using for-each when the loop needs the index — for-each gives the VALUE not the position; if you need to modify elements or access by index, must use regular indexed for loop; AP gives a task requiring index access

title: Class Structure — Instance Variables and Methods
objectives: private instance variables encapsulating state

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: initializes instance variables
accessor (get), mutator (set), others

traps: Declaring instance variables inside methods instead of the class body — instance variables belong to the object; variables in methods are local and lost when method returns; AP tests this scope distinction

title: Constructors and Method Overloading
objectives: Default constructor (no-arg) vs. parameterized constructor

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: same name, different parameter list
refers to the current object; disambiguates parameter and instance variable

traps: Not using this.variable = variable when parameter name matches instance variable name — without 'this', the assignment sets the local parameter equal to itself; AP gives a constructor where this is needed

title: Encapsulation and Information Hiding
objectives: Accessor/mutator pattern and when to include them

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: standard encapsulation
prevents invalid states

traps: Making instance variables public for convenience — violates encapsulation; AP FRQ explicitly tests writing proper private fields with public accessors and mutators

title: Static Variables and Methods
objectives: static belongs to the class, not individual instances

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: ClassName.method() preferred over object.method()
utility methods, class-level constants or counters

traps: Calling a static method on an instance variable — while it compiles, it's misleading; AP tests understanding that static methods don't have access to instance variables (no 'this' in static context)

title: Array Creation and Access
objectives: Index 0 to arr.length-1; ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException if violated
Array assignment creates alias (reference copy), not a value copy

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.term: int[] arr = new int[n]; default values
terms.def: 0, 0.0, false, null

traps: Thinking arr.length() is a method call — arrays use arr.length (no parentheses); String uses s.length() (method with parens); AP gives array access code and tests this syntax difference

title: Traversing Arrays — All Three Loop Types
objectives: Standard for loop with index for modification or random access

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: for(int x : arr)
last valid index is arr.length - 1

traps: Using for-each when the task requires modifying array elements — modifying 'x' in for(int x: arr) doesn't change the array; must use indexed loop: arr[i] = newValue; AP tests array modification requiring indexed access

title: Array Algorithms — Search and Sort
objectives: Finding max, min, sum, average in array traversal

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: O(n); binary search: O(log n) requires sorted array
O(n²)

traps: Applying binary search to an unsorted array — binary search only works on sorted arrays; AP gives an unsorted array and tests whether binary search would give the correct answer (it might not)

title: Passing Arrays to Methods
objectives: Returning an array from a method

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: method receives reference, changes affect original

terms.term: Array as a parameter vs. primitive parameter
terms.def: mutation visibility

traps: Assuming arrays are passed by value like primitives — a method that receives an array and modifies elements DOES modify the original array; AP tests whether changes made in a helper method are visible after the call

title: ArrayList vs. Array — When to Use Each
objectives: ArrayList is resizable; array has fixed size

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: ArrayList<Integer> not ArrayList<int>
add, get, set, remove, size

traps: Using ArrayList<int> — ArrayList requires an object type; must use the wrapper ArrayList<Integer>; autoboxing handles conversion automatically, but the type parameter must be Integer

title: ArrayList Traversal and Removal Pitfalls
objectives: for-each loop cannot be used when removing elements
ConcurrentModificationException when modifying during for-each iteration

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.term: Removing elements while iterating with index
terms.def: iterate backward or adjust index

traps: Removing from an ArrayList while iterating forward with an index — after removing at index i, the element that WAS at i+1 shifts to i; must decrement the loop counter after removal or iterate backward; AP tests this classic off-by-one with removal

title: ArrayList Methods and Autoboxing
objectives: Integer autoboxing and unboxing in ArrayList operations
Sublist and iterating a partial range

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: appends; list.add(i,e): inserts at index; list.remove(i): removes at index

traps: Confusing list.remove(int index) with list.remove(Object o) — list.remove(2) removes the element at index 2; list.remove(Integer.valueOf(2)) removes the first occurrence of value 2; AP tests this method overloading confusion

title: 2D Array Creation and Access
objectives: int[][] grid = new int[rows][cols]; row-major storage

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: grid[row][col]; grid.length = rows; grid[0].length = cols
rows can have different lengths

traps: Confusing row and column in 2D access — grid[i][j]: i is row (outer index), j is column (inner index); grid.length gives number of rows; grid[0].length gives number of columns; AP tests this frequently with matrix problems

title: Nested Loops for 2D Traversal
objectives: Master Nested Loops for 2D Traversal for the 2D Array unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: outer loop over rows, inner over columns
outer over columns, inner over rows
when row index = column index

traps: Accessing grid[col][row] instead of grid[row][col] in nested loops — the standard is outer = row = i, inner = col = j; reversing gives a transposed traversal; AP gives traversal code and asks what shape/pattern it produces

title: 2D Array Algorithms — Searching, Summing, Transforming
objectives: Row sum, column sum, diagonal sum patterns
Rotating a 2D array 90 degrees
Finding a value or computing a property across the entire grid

sections.title: 2D Array Algorithms — Searching, Summing, Transforming
traps: Using wrong bounds for partial traversal — summing the diagonal requires grid[i][i] with i from 0 to grid.length-1; summing a specific row requires grid[row][j] with j from 0 to grid[row].length-1; AP tests these specific traversal patterns

title: Extends and is-a Relationships
objectives: extends keyword; subclass inherits non-private members from superclass
formulas: Animal a=new Dog() → Dog override runs

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Dog is-a Animal; use for inheritance decisions
Car has-a Engine; use for composition

traps: Inheriting to reuse code when is-a doesn't hold — if the relationship is has-a, use composition (instance variable), not inheritance; AP tests whether a given relationship warrants inheritance or composition

title: Overriding vs. Overloading
objectives: Master Overriding vs. Overloading for the Inheritance unit.
formulas: Animal a=new Dog() → Dog override runs

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: same signature in subclass replaces superclass method
same name, different parameters in same class
prevents accidental overloading when intended to override

traps: Accidentally overloading instead of overriding — if parameter types differ even slightly, it's overloading; @Override causes a compile error if no matching method exists in superclass; AP tests code where the signature is slightly different

title: super Keyword and Constructor Chaining
objectives: super() must be first statement in subclass constructor
super.methodName() to call overridden superclass method
If no super() call, Java implicitly calls super() (no-arg constructor)
formulas: Animal a=new Dog() → Dog override runs

sections.title: super Keyword and Constructor Chaining
traps: Not calling super() when superclass has no default constructor — if the superclass only has a parameterized constructor, subclass constructor MUST explicitly call super(args); AP tests this with class hierarchies where superclass has only parameterized constructors

title: Polymorphism — Dynamic Dispatch at Runtime
objectives: Variable type (declared) determines what methods are visible at compile time
Object type (actual) determines which override is called at runtime
formulas: Animal a=new Dog() → Dog override runs

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Animal a = new Dog(); valid; Downcasting: Dog d = (Dog)a; may throw ClassCastException

traps: Confusing compile-time type with runtime type — Animal a = new Dog(); a.bark() is a compile error (Animal has no bark); but calling a.speak() uses Dog's override at runtime; AP tests both compile-time visibility and runtime dispatch

title: Recursion Fundamentals — Base Case and Recursive Case
objectives: Every recursive method needs a base case (no recursive call) and recursive case
Tracing recursive calls to find return value

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: each call adds a frame; returns unwind the stack

traps: Missing the base case or creating a base case that's never reached — infinite recursion → StackOverflowError; AP gives recursive code and asks for output when called with specific arguments, requiring careful trace

title: Tracing Recursive Methods
objectives: Drawing recursion tree or stack trace to follow execution
Return values propagate upward through the call chain

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: recursive call happens before return of calling frame

traps: Evaluating the return before the recursive call is fully resolved — must wait for inner calls to return before computing the outer return; AP gives a recursive method and asks for the exact return value of a call

title: Recursive vs. Iterative Solutions
objectives: Any iterative solution can be written recursively and vice versa
Recursion has call stack overhead; iteration has explicit stack management

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: tree traversal, divide-and-conquer, backtracking

traps: Writing recursive solutions that duplicate work — naive recursive Fibonacci recalculates the same values exponentially; memoization or iteration avoids this; AP may ask about time complexity of recursive vs. iterative Fibonacci

title: Recursive Array and String Processing
objectives: Master Recursive Array and String Processing for the Recursion unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: reverse, palindrome check, substring search
sum, search, min/max
process first element, recurse on rest

traps: Not correctly handling the base case for empty strings/arrays — an empty string has length 0; checking s.length() == 0 (or == 1) must be the base case; AP tests recursive string methods where the base case must return an identity value (empty string, 0, etc.)

title: Scarcity, Opportunity Cost, and the PPC
objectives: PPC shows maximum combinations of two goods — points ON curve are efficient

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: value of next best alternative given up — the true cost of any decision
resources or technology shift the curve; allocation choices move along it

traps: Drawing a PPC shift when the question shows a movement — a MOVEMENT along the PPC occurs when you reallocate existing resources; the CURVE SHIFTS only when total productive capacity changes (more resources, better technology); AP multiple choice frequently tests this distinction with a scenario requiring you to identify whether the change is a shift or movement

title: Comparative Advantage and Trade
objectives: Specialization and trade expanding consumption possibilities beyond the PPC

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: lower opportunity cost, not absolute production ability
mutually beneficial trade occurs between the two countries' opportunity costs

traps: Calculating comparative advantage using total output instead of opportunity cost — ALWAYS convert to opportunity cost (what you give up of one good to produce one more of the other); the country with the LOWER opportunity cost has comparative advantage; a common AP trap: one country has absolute advantage in both goods but each has comparative advantage in one — both still benefit from trade

unitName: Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle
title: GDP — Measuring National Output
objectives: Master GDP — Measuring National Output for the Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: GDP = C + I + G + NX — memorize and know what each includes/excludes
nominal uses current prices; real adjusts for inflation using base year prices
intermediate goods, non-market production, underground economy, income distribution

traps: Including intermediate goods in GDP calculations — GDP counts FINAL goods only to avoid double-counting; if you count steel AND the car made from it, you've counted the steel twice; AP free response frequently requires identifying what IS and IS NOT included in GDP; memorize the exclusions (used goods, financial transactions, transfer payments) as carefully as the inclusions

unitName: Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle
title: Unemployment — Types and Measurement
objectives: Natural rate of unemployment = frictional + structural (NOT zero unemployment)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: between jobs (normal, unavoidable); structural: skills mismatch; cyclical: recession-caused

terms.term: Labor force participation rate vs. unemployment rate
terms.def: discouraged workers leaving labor force REDUCES the measured rate

traps: Treating full employment as zero unemployment — full employment means NO CYCLICAL unemployment, but frictional and structural persist; the natural rate (about 4-5%) IS full employment; AP tests that reducing frictional unemployment (better job-matching services) lowers the natural rate; reducing cyclical unemployment is the goal of stabilization policy — these are different policy targets

unitName: Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle
title: Inflation — Measurement and Effects
objectives: Master Inflation — Measurement and Effects for the Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: fixed basket of goods measuring price level change for consumers
hurts lenders (paid back in less valuable dollars); helps borrowers
extreme inflation destroying the medium of exchange function of money (Germany 1923)

traps: Treating all inflation as equally bad — AP tests the DISTRIBUTIONAL effects: unexpected inflation transfers wealth from lenders to borrowers; anticipated inflation is built into interest rates and causes less disruption; deflation is ALSO harmful (delays purchases, increases real debt burden); the AP macro question is usually about unexpected inflation's effects on specific groups, requiring you to identify who holds assets vs. owes debts

title: Aggregate Demand — The AD Curve
objectives: AD = C + I + G + NX — same components as GDP but showing quantity demanded at each price level

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: wealth effect, interest rate effect, foreign purchases effect
changes in C, I, G, NX that are NOT caused by price level changes

traps: Confusing a movement along AD with a shift — price level changes MOVE you along the AD curve (same curve, different point); only NON-PRICE-LEVEL factors shift AD (consumer confidence, government spending, foreign income); this is the most common error on AP macro; in free response, always state whether you're showing a shift (draw new curve) or movement (show point moving on existing curve)

title: Aggregate Supply — Short Run and Long Run
objectives: Master Aggregate Supply — Short Run and Long Run for the National Income and Price Determination unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: higher prices make production more profitable in short run (input costs sticky)

terms.term: LRAS is vertical at full employment
terms.def: in long run, all prices adjust, so output returns to natural level
input prices, supply shocks; LRAS shifts: changes in productive capacity

traps: Drawing SRAS when you mean LRAS — a key AP trap: 'supply-side policies' that increase LRAS (more workers, better technology) are different from expansionary fiscal policy that increases AD; AP free response specifically tests whether you correctly draw LRAS as vertical; a non-vertical LRAS costs you the graphing point; practice drawing the three-curve AS-AD model until vertical LRAS is automatic

title: The Multiplier Effect
objectives: Spending multiplier = 1/(1-MPC) = 1/MPS — larger MPC means larger multiplier
Tax multiplier = -MPC/(1-MPC) — smaller than spending multiplier because first dollar of tax cut is partly saved
Balanced budget multiplier = 1 — equal increase in G and T increases GDP by the same amount

sections.title: The Multiplier Effect
traps: Using the spending multiplier for tax changes — the TAX MULTIPLIER is smaller in magnitude than the spending multiplier (MPC/MPS vs. 1/MPS) because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved; AP free response frequently asks you to calculate both and explain why they differ; the balanced budget multiplier (= 1) showing that equal G and T increases raise GDP is a classic multiple choice trap

title: Short-Run Equilibrium vs. Long-Run Self-Correction
objectives: Master Short-Run Equilibrium vs. Long-Run Self-Correction for the National Income and Price Determination unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: equilibrium output below full employment — wages eventually fall, SRAS shifts right
output above potential — wages eventually rise, SRAS shifts left back to LRAS
without policy, the economy eventually returns to LRAS

traps: Forgetting to show the self-correction when asked about long-run outcomes — AP free response asking 'what happens in the long run' requires showing SRAS shifting to restore LRAS equilibrium; the sequence is: gap identified → wage adjustment → SRAS shifts → new long-run equilibrium at LRAS; missing any step of this sequence loses graphing and explanation points

title: Money — Functions, Supply, and Demand
objectives: Master Money — Functions, Supply, and Demand for the Financial Sector unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account
M1 (cash + checking deposits); M2 (M1 + savings + money market)
transaction demand (rises with GDP) + asset demand (falls as interest rates rise)

traps: Treating the money market graph like a regular supply/demand model — the money SUPPLY is vertical (set by the Fed, not price-sensitive); money DEMAND slopes downward because higher interest rates make holding non-interest cash more costly; the equilibrium interest rate is where they meet; AP specifically tests shifting money supply right (lower interest rate) vs. left (higher rate) as the mechanism of monetary policy

title: Banking and Money Creation
objectives: Required reserve ratio determining the money multiplier = 1/RRR

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: bank loans creating deposits creating more loans (the multiplier process)
the rate banks charge each other for overnight reserve loans — the Fed's key policy instrument

traps: Confusing the money multiplier with the spending multiplier — MONEY multiplier = 1/RRR (reserve ratio); SPENDING multiplier = 1/MPS (marginal propensity to save); AP tests both in the same exam; the money multiplier tells you the maximum new money from a deposit; in practice the actual increase is less because banks hold excess reserves and people hold cash outside the banking system — AP tests this 'leakage'

title: The Federal Reserve and Monetary Policy
objectives: Master The Federal Reserve and Monetary Policy for the Financial Sector unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: lower federal funds rate → increased investment → AD shifts right
raise federal funds rate → less investment → AD shifts left
open market operations (primary), discount rate, reserve requirements

traps: Stopping the monetary policy chain at 'lower interest rates' — AP free response requires the FULL chain: Fed buys bonds → bank reserves increase → federal funds rate falls → investment increases → AD shifts right → real GDP increases, unemployment falls, price level rises; each link in the chain is worth points; stopping at 'more money in economy' without tracing through interest rates to AD earns partial credit

title: Fiscal Policy — Government Spending and Taxation
objectives: Master Fiscal Policy — Government Spending and Taxation for the Long-Run Consequences of Stabilization Policies unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: increase G or decrease T → shifts AD right
decrease G or increase T → shifts AD left
government borrowing driving up interest rates, reducing private investment

traps: Ignoring crowding out in fiscal policy analysis — when the government borrows to fund spending, it COMPETES for loanable funds with private borrowers, raising interest rates and reducing investment; AP free response specifically asks about crowding out as a limitation of fiscal policy; a complete answer traces: deficit spending → increased demand for loanable funds → higher interest rates → reduced investment → partially offsets AD increase

title: Phillips Curve — Short Run and Long Run
objectives: Master Phillips Curve — Short Run and Long Run for the Long-Run Consequences of Stabilization Policies unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment
vertical at natural rate of unemployment (no long-run tradeoff)
both inflation and unemployment rising simultaneously

traps: Treating the Phillips curve as a permanent policy menu — AP tests that the short-run tradeoff is TEMPORARY; increasing AD to lower unemployment causes inflation, but workers adjust wage expectations, shifting SRPC upward; the long-run result is higher inflation at the SAME unemployment rate; stagflation (1970s) proved this — policy makers learned they couldn't permanently buy lower unemployment with higher inflation

unitName: Open Economy — International Trade and Finance
title: Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates
objectives: Master Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates for the Open Economy — International Trade and Finance unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: trade in goods/services + income + transfers (the 'real' economy flows)
investment flows — must balance with current account
determined by supply and demand for currencies

traps: Confusing appreciation with depreciation effects on trade — currency APPRECIATION makes exports more expensive (foreigners buy less) and imports cheaper (domestic consumers buy more) → worsens trade balance; DEPRECIATION does the opposite; AP traces this full chain; the common error is stopping at 'exchange rate changes' without connecting to how it affects the trade balance through relative prices

unitName: Open Economy — International Trade and Finance
title: Exchange Rate Policy and International Effects
objectives: Higher domestic interest rates attracting foreign capital → currency appreciates

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: Fed raises rates → dollar appreciates → net exports fall → partially offsets AD expansion
tradeoffs in policy autonomy vs. stability

traps: Forgetting the exchange rate effect in monetary policy analysis — when the Fed raises interest rates, foreign investors demand dollars to invest → dollar APPRECIATES → US exports become more expensive → net exports FALL → this PARTIALLY OFFSETS the contractionary effect on domestic investment; AP free response awards a separate point for correctly tracing monetary policy through the exchange rate to net exports — most students miss this point

title: Scarcity, Opportunity Cost, and Marginal Analysis
objectives: Master Scarcity, Opportunity Cost, and Marginal Analysis for the Basic Economic Concepts unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: decisions made at the margin, not totals — 'one more unit' thinking
already incurred, should NOT affect future decisions
choose an action when marginal benefit ≥ marginal cost

traps: Using total cost/benefit instead of marginal in optimization problems — AP micro tests MARGINAL thinking in almost every context; the optimal production level is where MC = MR (not total profit maximum); the optimal consumption is where MB = MC; sunk costs appearing in a scenario are a deliberate trap — always ask 'what changes going forward?' and ignore what's already spent

title: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
objectives: Price ceiling below equilibrium → shortage; price floor above equilibrium → surplus

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: income, prices of related goods, expectations, tastes, number of buyers
input prices, technology, number of sellers, expectations

traps: Drawing the wrong direction for a supply shift caused by input price increases — higher input prices DECREASE supply (shift left) because it's more costly to produce; AP tests the direction of shifts with subtle scenarios; a useful check: if production becomes more costly or less profitable for any reason, supply decreases; if more profitable or less costly, supply increases

unitName: Supply and Demand — Consumer and Producer Theory
title: Elasticity — Price, Income, and Cross-Price
objectives: PED = %ΔQd / %ΔP — elastic demand (>1) means revenue falls when price rises

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: positive = normal good; negative = inferior good
positive = substitutes; negative = complements

traps: Calculating elasticity using absolute values without specifying direction — AP awards full credit when you correctly identify whether demand is elastic or inelastic AND connect it to total revenue; elastic demand: price ↑ → revenue ↓ (opposite direction); inelastic: price ↑ → revenue ↑ (same direction); the total revenue test is faster than calculation for multiple choice and AP expects you to use it

unitName: Supply and Demand — Consumer and Producer Theory
title: Consumer Surplus, Producer Surplus, and Efficiency
objectives: Master Consumer Surplus, Producer Surplus, and Efficiency for the Supply and Demand — Consumer and Producer Theory unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: area above price and below demand curve
area below price and above supply curve
loss of total surplus from quantity not produced at efficient level

traps: Drawing deadweight loss on the wrong side — DWL is the triangle BETWEEN the efficient quantity and the actual quantity; for a binding price ceiling (below equilibrium), the DWL triangle points right (toward higher quantities that would have been traded); for a price floor, same logic; for a tax, DWL is between the buyer price and seller price at the new quantity; incorrect DWL placement loses the graphing point

unitName: Supply and Demand — Consumer and Producer Theory
title: Government Interventions — Taxes, Subsidies, Price Controls
objectives: Master Government Interventions — Taxes, Subsidies, Price Controls for the Supply and Demand — Consumer and Producer Theory unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: burden falls more on inelastic side (buyers or sellers)
wedge between buyer price and seller price equal to the tax amount
shifts supply right; benefits split between buyers and sellers based on elasticity

traps: Assuming tax burden falls on whoever the tax is imposed on — AP tests ECONOMIC incidence, not statutory incidence; if a tax is placed on sellers but demand is perfectly inelastic, buyers bear the full burden (price rises by full tax); tax incidence depends on relative elasticities, not who writes the check to the government; drawing the tax wedge correctly and identifying which side bears more burden is a standard AP free response task

unitName: Production, Cost, and the Perfect Competition Model
title: Production and Costs in the Short Run
objectives: Fixed costs (don't change with output) vs. variable costs (change with output)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: adding workers to fixed capital reduces each worker's additional output
when MP rises, MC falls; when MP falls, MC rises — they mirror each other

traps: Forgetting the inverse relationship between MP and MC — when marginal product of labor is RISING (early workers are more productive as they specialize), marginal cost is FALLING; when MP starts falling (diminishing returns), MC starts rising; the AP graph question almost always shows both curves and tests whether you understand they are mirror images through the production function

unitName: Production, Cost, and the Perfect Competition Model
title: Perfect Competition — Short-Run and Long-Run Equilibrium
objectives: Master Perfect Competition — Short-Run and Long-Run Equilibrium for the Production, Cost, and the Perfect Competition Model unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: perfectly competitive firm takes market price as given (horizontal demand curve)
produce where P = MR = MC
P = MC = ATC (zero economic profit, maximum efficiency)

traps: Confusing economic profit with accounting profit — AP tests ECONOMIC profit which subtracts implicit costs (opportunity cost of owner's time and capital); zero economic profit means normal profit (owner earning what they could elsewhere); a firm earning zero economic profit will STAY in the industry; only firms earning NEGATIVE economic profit (below normal return) will exit; this distinction drives long-run adjustment

unitName: Production, Cost, and the Perfect Competition Model
title: Shutdown and Break-Even Decisions
objectives: Shut down in short run if P < AVC (not covering variable costs)
Exit in long run if P < ATC (not covering all costs including fixed)
Firm continues operating in short run even at a loss as long as P ≥ AVC

sections.title: Shutdown and Break-Even Decisions
traps: Confusing short-run shutdown with long-run exit — in the SHORT RUN a firm should CONTINUE operating if P ≥ AVC because fixed costs are sunk; shutting down saves variable costs but loses revenue; in the LONG RUN all costs are variable, so exit if P < ATC; AP tests this distinction with 'should the firm shut down immediately or exit the industry?' — they require different cost comparisons

title: Monopoly — Market Power and Inefficiency
objectives: Monopolist faces downward-sloping demand — must lower price to sell more, making MR < P

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: MR = MC; then charge the price consumers will pay (from demand curve)
monopolist produces less than socially optimal quantity

traps: Drawing the monopoly profit-maximizing price on the MC curve instead of the demand curve — the monopolist produces where MR = MC (that's the QUANTITY), then charges the price from the DEMAND CURVE at that quantity (that's the PRICE); never read price from MC; this two-step process is tested in almost every AP micro free response involving monopoly; practice until it's automatic

title: Monopolistic Competition — Differentiation and Long Run
objectives: Product differentiation creating downward-sloping demand for each firm

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: can earn profit or loss; Long run: zero profit (like perfect competition)
tangent to ATC — excess capacity (not at minimum ATC)

traps: Forgetting to show excess capacity in monopolistic competition long-run graph — the tangency point where demand touches ATC is to the LEFT of minimum ATC; this means the firm is NOT producing at minimum average cost, creating 'excess capacity'; AP specifically tests this as the inefficiency of monopolistic competition; contrasting it with perfect competition (which produces at minimum ATC) is a standard comparison question

title: Oligopoly — Game Theory and Strategic Behavior
objectives: Master Oligopoly — Game Theory and Strategic Behavior for the Imperfect Competition unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: individually rational choices producing collectively bad outcomes
each player choosing best response given what others are doing
firms acting like a monopolist; price leadership as tacit collusion

traps: Treating game theory questions as just about the specific example — AP tests the GENERAL PRINCIPLE: in a prisoner's dilemma, the dominant strategy leads to a Nash equilibrium that is WORSE for both players than cooperation would be; applying this to pricing cartels, advertising, or arms races requires understanding that self-interest undermining collective interest is the core insight; firms will cheat on cartel agreements for the same reason prisoners defect

title: Labor Markets — MRP and Wage Determination
objectives: MRP = MP × Product price — the derived demand for labor
Firm hires labor until MRP = wage (MRC)

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: single buyer of labor setting wage below competitive level

traps: Treating factor markets exactly like product markets — labor demand is DERIVED demand (derived from product demand); if product price rises, MRP rises, and the firm hires more labor at the same wage; AP tests the connection between product markets and factor markets: a tax on the firm's product reduces its MRP, shifting labor demand left; factor market analysis requires tracing through the product market first

unitName: Market Failure and the Role of Government
title: Externalities and Public Goods
objectives: Master Externalities and Public Goods for the Market Failure and the Role of Government unit.

sections.title: Key concepts

terms.def: social cost > private cost → market overproduces; Pigouvian tax corrects it
social benefit > private benefit → market underproduces; subsidy corrects it
non-excludable + non-rival → free rider problem → private market underprovides

traps: Drawing externality graphs without showing the social cost/benefit curve — AP free response requires drawing BOTH the private and social curves; for negative externality: supply (private cost) is below the true social cost curve; efficient output is where demand meets SOCIAL cost, which is LESS than market output; for positive externality: demand (private benefit) is below social benefit; draw both curves, mark the market quantity and efficient quantity, and shade the deadweight loss triangle
